texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Taskforce Mandate
texts.text: Taskforce Mandate

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The overall mandate of the Taskforce was to advise the Cabinet Secretary on issues, policies and strategies that the education sector needs to address in order to enhance access, relevance, transition, equity and quality for effective curriculum reforms implementation.
texts.text: The overall mandate of the Taskforce was to advise the Cabinet Secretary on issues, policies and strategies that the education sector needs to address in order to enhance access, relevance, transition, equity and quality for effective curriculum reforms implementation.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Terms of Reference
texts.text: Terms of Reference

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1.  Undertake broad stakeholder engagement, review literature and identify international best practices with a view to preparing a comprehensive advisory report on:
texts.text: Undertake broad stakeholder engagement, review literature and identify international best practices with a view to preparing a comprehensive advisory report on:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: a.  Transition of Grade 6 cohort (of CBC) and Standard 7 and 8 (of 8-4-4) pupils in 2023.
texts.text: Transition of Grade 6 cohort (of CBC) and Standard 7 and 8 (of 8-4-4) pupils in 2023.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: b.  Domiciling of Grade 7, 8 and 9 within the Basic Education Structure.
texts.text: Domiciling of Grade 7, 8 and 9 within the Basic Education Structure.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: c.  Competency Based Assessment for the reformed curriculum.
texts.text: Competency Based Assessment for the reformed curriculum.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: d.  Identification of schools to host the Pathways and Tracks in Senior Secondary School, while considering equity and cost effectiveness.
texts.text: Identification of schools to host the Pathways and Tracks in Senior Secondary School, while considering equity and cost effectiveness.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: e.  Strategies and work plans to prepare the country for implementation of Senior Secondary School  Pathways  and  Tracks  in  2026,  including  infrastructural  and  human  resource requirements.
texts.text: Strategies and work plans to prepare the country for implementation of Senior Secondary School  Pathways  and  Tracks  in  2026,  including  infrastructural  and  human  resource requirements.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: f.  Conceptualization and design of competency based pre-service teacher education.
texts.text: Conceptualization and design of competency based pre-service teacher education.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: g.  Design and implementation of Value-Based Education; Community Service Learning; and Parental Empowerment and Engagement programmes.
texts.text: Design and implementation of Value-Based Education; Community Service Learning; and Parental Empowerment and Engagement programmes.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: h.  Transition from Basic to Tertiary Education and Training in 2029, including infrastructural and human resource requirements.
texts.text: Transition from Basic to Tertiary Education and Training in 2029, including infrastructural and human resource requirements.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 2.  Advise on policy and legal issues necessary for effective implementation of the curriculum reforms,  including  a  framework  on  the  working  relationship  between  the  national  and county governments on implementation of the Pre-primary school curriculum.
texts.text: Advise on policy and legal issues necessary for effective implementation of the curriculum reforms,  including  a  framework  on  the  working  relationship  between  the  national  and county governments on implementation of the Pre-primary school curriculum.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 3.  Prepare a strategy for monitoring and evaluation of the curriculum reforms implementation.
texts.text: Prepare a strategy for monitoring and evaluation of the curriculum reforms implementation.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 4.  Advise  on  any  other  relevant  issue  for  effective  and  efficient  implementation  of  the curriculum reforms.
texts.text: Advise  on  any  other  relevant  issue  for  effective  and  efficient  implementation  of  the curriculum reforms.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 5. Prepare periodic and a final Taskforce report.
texts.text: Prepare periodic and a final Taskforce report.

texts.orig: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE CBC IMPLEMENTATION REPORT
texts.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE CBC IMPLEMENTATION REPORT

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: I: Overview
texts.text: I: Overview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This executive summary encapsulates the key issues and related recommendations that will enhance effective implementation of the Competency Based Curriculum (CBC) reforms as stipulated in the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (KICD, 2017), Competency Based Assessment Framework (CBAF) and respective curriculum designs and programmes. In this context, the Taskforce on Enhancing Access, Relevance, Transition, Equity and Quality for Effective Curriculum Reforms Implementation interpreted and responded to each of its Terms of  Reference  (ToR)  within  the  overall  mandate  of  advising  the  Cabinet  Secretary  (CS), Ministry of Education (MoE), on issues , policies and strategies that the education sector needs to  address  in  order  to  ensure  access,  relevance,  transition,  equity  and  quality  for  effective curriculum reforms implementation.
texts.text: This executive summary encapsulates the key issues and related recommendations that will enhance effective implementation of the Competency Based Curriculum (CBC) reforms as stipulated in the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (KICD, 2017), Competency Based Assessment Framework (CBAF) and respective curriculum designs and programmes. In this context, the Taskforce on Enhancing Access, Relevance, Transition, Equity and Quality for Effective Curriculum Reforms Implementation interpreted and responded to each of its Terms of  Reference  (ToR)  within  the  overall  mandate  of  advising  the  Cabinet  Secretary  (CS), Ministry of Education (MoE), on issues , policies and strategies that the education sector needs to  address  in  order  to  ensure  access,  relevance,  transition,  equity  and  quality  for  effective curriculum reforms implementation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The executive summary presents highlights of the Taskforce Report in line with the ToR on transition  of  Primary  Grade  6  learners  to  Junior  Secondary  School  (JSS)  Grade  7  and domiciling of JSS Grades 7, 8 and 9 within the Basic Education structure; Transition of JSS learners to Senior Secondary School (SSS) Grades 10, 11 and 12; Transition from Basic to Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET); Transition from Basic to University Education;  positioning  Special  Needs  Education  (SNE)  within  the  BECF  (KICD,  2017); foregrounding Competency Based Assessment (CBA) at all levels of learning for all learners; conceptualizing and designing Competency Based Teacher Education (CBTE).
texts.text: The executive summary presents highlights of the Taskforce Report in line with the ToR on transition  of  Primary  Grade  6  learners  to  Junior  Secondary  School  (JSS)  Grade  7  and domiciling of JSS Grades 7, 8 and 9 within the Basic Education structure; Transition of JSS learners to Senior Secondary School (SSS) Grades 10, 11 and 12; Transition from Basic to Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET); Transition from Basic to University Education;  positioning  Special  Needs  Education  (SNE)  within  the  BECF  (KICD,  2017); foregrounding Competency Based Assessment (CBA) at all levels of learning for all learners; conceptualizing and designing Competency Based Teacher Education (CBTE).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The executive  summary also addresses the design and implementation of Parental Empowerment  and  Engagement  (PEE),  Value-Based  (VBE)  Education  and  Community Service Learning (CSL) Programmes; synopsis of policy and legal issues to support effective curriculum reforms implementation; fronting a Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) Strategy and  Framework  for  the  CBC;  underscoring  the  need  for  a  strong  Standards  and  Quality Assurance (SQA) system for Basic Education and Training programmes; positioning the role of good Governance, Financing and Integration of Information Communication Technology (ICT)    for  effective  implementation  of  the  curriculum  reforms;  as  well  as  the  need  for  a comprehensive Communication Strategy on the curriculum reforms implementation.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: II: Transitioning and Domiciling of Junior Secondary School (JSS)
texts.text: II: Transitioning and Domiciling of Junior Secondary School (JSS)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: JSS Grades 7, 8 and 9 will be domiciled at the Secondary education level. This is informed by the fact that it is at JSS that learners will need to deepen their understanding of the broad CBC curriculum and choose the Pathways and Tracks to follow in SSS. The Primary school level lacks capacity, both in human resource and infrastructure (especially for teaching sciences), to facilitate the expected depth of engagement with the JSS CBC content. Further, domiciling JSS at Secondary school level will optimize teacher utilization as they will teach at both JSS and SSS levels. This recommendation is aligned with the practice in other Countries within the East African Community (EAC) and international best practices.
texts.text: JSS Grades 7, 8 and 9 will be domiciled at the Secondary education level. This is informed by the fact that it is at JSS that learners will need to deepen their understanding of the broad CBC curriculum and choose the Pathways and Tracks to follow in SSS. The Primary school level lacks capacity, both in human resource and infrastructure (especially for teaching sciences), to facilitate the expected depth of engagement with the JSS CBC content. Further, domiciling JSS at Secondary school level will optimize teacher utilization as they will teach at both JSS and SSS levels. This recommendation is aligned with the practice in other Countries within the East African Community (EAC) and international best practices.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Learners who, in 2022, will be in Primary school (Grade 6) under the 2-6-6-3 CBC and those in Standard 8 of the 8-4-4 education system will concurrently transition to JSS Grade 7 and Secondary Form 1, respectively. For effective- transition from Primary to Secondary education of the CBC and 8-4-4 cohorts and domiciling of JSS in the Basic Education structure, critical issues that will influence the double transitions need to be addressed. These include: a 27% increase in Secondary school learner population in Year 2023 from 4,381,701 to 6,029,168; trends  of increased  transition from  Primary  school  between  2023  and  2025;  learner characteristics at transition which include changes in psycho -social maturity and age decline from  an  average  of  14-year-olds  to  12-year-olds;  need  for  expansion  of  Secondary  school human resource and infrastructure as well as funding of the Secondary education level. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Implementation of the Pathways and Tracks at SSS in 2026, while considering equity and cost effectiveness, raises the issue of adequate preparations in terms of infrastructure and human resources (especially physical infrastructure for  Science  Technology  Engineering  and Mathematics (STEM) and teachers for new learning areas (such as Sports Science). This is in the context of the BECF (KICD, 2017) which proposes that 60 per cent of the learners at SSS will pursue the 4 Tracks in the STEM Pathway. The remaining 25 per cent of learners will pursue  Languages  and  Social  Sciences,  while  15  per  cent  will  pursue  Sports  Science, Performing and Visual Arts. In this context, the Taskforce recommends implementation of the following strategies and policies respectively :

texts.orig: VI: Special Needs Education is an integral part of CBC, especially in view of the Mission of Nurturing Every Learner's Potential ,  including the Gifted and Talented. Although the SNE sub-sector has experienced tremendous growth over the years, there are issues that need to be addressed for effective implementation of the CBC. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Assessment at Primary level will be mainly formative. In Grades 1 to 3, teachers will conduct classroom assessment, and at Grade 3, KNEC will develop standardized assessment tools to be administered, scored and feedback given to individual learners by teachers in their respective schools. Schools will then submit the results for each learner in a designated format to KNEC to facilitate analysis of achievement of competencies at national level. The report from KNEC will guide the teachers receiving the transitioning Grade 4 and to advise the TSC in developing content for continuous Teacher Professional Development (TPD) that targets areas requiring intervention. Further, KICD will use the report to develop instructional resources that target areas that learners may find challenging as well as to revise the curriculum in cases where assessment reports reveal that the curriculum could be the cause of weak achievement.

texts.orig: Assessment in upper Primary will align to a policy governing the balance between formative and  summative,  to  assess  comprehensively,  the  mastery  of multifarious  competencies  of different learners as well as to facilitate placement of learners in JSS. The mode of assessment will entail a combination of teacher-administered formative assessment in Grades 4, 5 and 6, and a summative assessment to be administered by KNEC at the end of Grade 6. The proposed weighting  is  60%  for  formative  and  40%  for  summative  assessment. The  summative assessment is prompted by the need to allow learners across the Country to access schools which have superior infrastructure and a culture of good performance, thus enhancing equity.

texts.orig: XIII: Governance, Financing and Integration of ICT
texts.text: XIII: Governance, Financing and Integration of ICT

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Governance,  financing  and  integration  of  ICT  in  the  education  sector  will  be  critical  for efficient  and  effective  implementation  of  the  CBC.  There  is  need  for  transformations  in teaching and learning processes based on new pedagogies that are appropriate for the 21st Century skills that requires leveraging on ICT integration.  This has potential to improve not only the quality of educational administration and delivery of programmes and services but also enhance education access, equity and quality. The Taskforce addresses the pertinent issues thematically and makes recommendations accordingly.

texts.orig: 1.2.1 Education in the Context of Constitution of Kenya 2010
texts.text: 1.2.1 Education in the Context of Constitution of Kenya 2010

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Taskforce focused on the role of education, and especially curriculum reforms as critical for effective continued implementation of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) and achievement of the dictates of the Kenya Vision 2030. The Taskforce also took cognizance of the global and regional educational reforms that that have a bearing on the national reforms. It is in this context that this Taskforce  was  mandated  to  provide  advice  on  enhancing  effective  curriculum  reforms implementation. The contextual foci are highlighted as follows.
texts.text: The Taskforce focused on the role of education, and especially curriculum reforms as critical for effective continued implementation of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) and achievement of the dictates of the Kenya Vision 2030. The Taskforce also took cognizance of the global and regional educational reforms that that have a bearing on the national reforms. It is in this context that this Taskforce  was  mandated  to  provide  advice  on  enhancing  effective  curriculum  reforms implementation. The contextual foci are highlighted as follows.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Kenya Constitution (2010) reflects a culmination of five (5) decades of consistent focus of educational  developments.  It  provides  for  the  right  of  every  person  to  achieve  the  highest attainable standard of education, training and research and assigns different aspects of education, training  and  research  to  both  the  National  and  County  Governments.  This  constitutional arrangement creates opportunity for sharing functions between the two levels of Government which jointly serve the Kenyan child at different levels of the education system. Article 53 (1) (b) states that every child has a right to free and compulsory Basic Education, while Article 55 (a) obligates the State to take measures, including affirmative action programmes, to ensure that the youth access relevant education and training.

texts.orig: The East African Community (EAC) treaty, especially its agreements on education, has greatly influenced educational reforms in Kenya in ways that have shaped the focus of this Taskforce. The EAC is a regional inter-governmental organisation  of six  (6)  Partner  States,  comprising Burundi,  Kenya,  Rwanda,  South  Sudan,  Tanzania  and  Uganda  thus  giving  it  the  status  with potential for enhancing inter-governmental synergies in education.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Treaty that established the EAC was signed on 30 th November 1999 and enforced on 7 th July 2000 following its ratification by the original three Partner States; Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. The Republic of Rwanda and the Republic of Burundi acceded to the EAC Treaty on 18 th June 2007  and  became  full  members  of  the  Community  with  effect  from  1 st July  2007  while  the Republic of South Sudan became a full member in 2016.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1.3 Highlights from previous commissions, committees, taskforces and working parties on education in Kenya
texts.text: 1.3 Highlights from previous commissions, committees, taskforces and working parties on education in Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Immediately after Kenya attained its political independence in 1963, education became one of its priority areas for which the Country has had several Commissions. Each of the Commissions recommended different policies that created various opportunities, some of which have never been fully implemented, particularly in the area of moral values education. Further, most of the Commission reports stressed the need for curriculum reforms that would help learners to gain practical skills and competences for self-reliance and that have relevance in the labour market.

texts.orig: 1.3.1 The Kenya Education Commission of 1964 (The Ominde Report)
texts.text: 1.3.1 The Kenya Education Commission of 1964 (The Ominde Report)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ominde Report (GoK, 1964) sought to reform colonial education to reflect the nation's sovereignty.  It  therefore  advocated  for  national  unity  and  the  development  of  the  necessary human resource to steer socio-cultural and economic development through a unified national curriculum  as  opposed  to  the  stratified  racial system  that  restricted  black  Africans  to industrial/technical and vocational education. Changes recommended included subject content for  History  and  Geography  to  reflect  national  cohesion.  The  7-4-2-3-system  was  adopted  to capture seven years of Primary, four years of lower Secondary (Form 1-4), two years of upper Secondary (Form 5-6), and a minimum three years of University education.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1.4.1.3 Needs Assessment for Curriculum Reform (KICD, 2016)
texts.text: 1.4.1.3 Needs Assessment for Curriculum Reform (KICD, 2016)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The KICD carried out a national needs assessment study in order to confirm the issues raised by the  Odhiambo  Report  (MoE,  2012),  while  also  identifying  other  issues  that  required  to  be addressed  in  the  anticipated  reforms.  Generally,  the  needs  assessment  study  revealed  that Kenyans desired a major reform of the education structure and school curriculum to emphasize acquisition of relevant competencies, talent identification and nurturing, adoption of effective pedagogical  approaches,  resources  and  assessment.  Kenyans  expressed  the  need  for  the curriculum  to  be  reformed  to  enhance  peaceful  social  co-existence,  contribute  to  economic development and to negate social vices such as corruption, tribalism and insecurity. They also expressed  a  desire  for  a  curriculum  that  promotes  national  unity  and  cohesion  innovation, problem solving and self-reliance for improving individual and national development.

texts.orig: 2.1 Introduction
texts.text: 2.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter focusses on transition from Primary school in Grade 6 to Junior Secondary School (JSS) level in Grade 7 under the 2-6-6-3 structure of education. It also discusses the domiciling of JSS (Grades 7, 8 and 9), which is one of the new levels in the Basic Education structure as designed in the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECF, KICD, 2017). The chapter is organised in 6 main sections excluding this introduction. The first section addresses key concepts used in the chapter followed by a situational analysis of the school enrolments, infrastructure, funding, teaching workforce and learner characteristics at the critical level of transition to JSS. The next section explores international best practices on transition to JSS as well as domiciling of the same. This is followed by insights from stakeholder submissions and engagements. Finally, the chapter presents recommendations derived from the various issues of focus.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.2.2 Junior Secondary School
texts.text: 2.2.2 Junior Secondary School

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the context of the 2-6-6-3 education structure, JSS (also referred to as Lower Secondary in other education systems) is the phase of learning between Primary school and SSS, targeting learners in the age bracket of 12 to 14 years (Odhiambo Report, MoE, 2012). According to the BECF (KICD, 2017), learners in JSS will be exposed to a broad-based curriculum to enable them explore their abilities, personalities, interests and potentials. This forms the basis for effective identification of career paths, talents and interests in preparation for transition to SSS.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.2.3 Domiciling of Junior Secondary within Basic Education Structure
texts.text: 2.2.3 Domiciling of Junior Secondary within Basic Education Structure

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Domiciling  in  the  context  of  the  education  reforms  and  the  Taskforce  ToR  refers  to  the conceptual and/or infrastructural (human and physical) environment in which JSS (Grades 7, 8 and 9) will be hosted. Secondary education in the 2-6-6-3 system is divided into two: JSS (3 years comprising Grades 7 - 9) and SSS (3 years; Grades 10 - 12) unlike in the 8-4-4 system where  this  comprised  four  continuous  years  of  learning.  Comparatively,  in  most  Countries, learners spend between six and seven years at Primary school level, and on average, six years at Secondary school level, usually divided into two (Junior and Senior) as shown in Table 2.2.

Further, in Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, the Secondary school cycle is divided into 2 to allow learners experience a broad curriculum before subject specialization at SSS level. As  a  signatory  to  the  EAC  protocol  on  harmonisation  of  the  education  curricula,  standards, assessment and evaluation of education programmes, this signals a need to realign the Kenya education system with the rest of East Africa. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.2.4 Access, Equity, Relevance and Quality in Secondary Education
texts.text: 2.2.4 Access, Equity, Relevance and Quality in Secondary Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Access to and equity in Secondary education are primarily addressed through enrolment in terms of:  adequacy  and  availability  of  opportunities,  infrastructure  and  resources;  being  matters  of global concern, particularly in Africa.
texts.text: Access to and equity in Secondary education are primarily addressed through enrolment in terms of:  adequacy  and  availability  of  opportunities,  infrastructure  and  resources;  being  matters  of global concern, particularly in Africa.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The experiences in sub-Saharan African Countries show that access heavily influences the trends in transition from Primary to Secondary schooling (UNESCO, 2017). According to World Bank (2008),  the  demand  for  Secondary  education  has  risen  rapidly  in  Africa,  and  enrolment  has expanded exponentially, with the demand surpassing the available spaces. The report states that Secondary school enrolment in African Countries averages only 30 per cent, compared to 65 per cent for developing Countries, and about 100 per cent in East Asia. In addition, on average, only 30 per cent of each cohort completes Junior Secondary education in sub-Saharan Africa. Studies by Lewin (2008); UIS (2005b); and Clemens (2004) pointed out that the probability of entering Secondary school also significantly influences the demand for Primary education.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Odhiambo Report (MoE, 2012) defines access in terms of Gross Enrolment Ratios (GERs), Net Enrolment Ratios (NERs), transition, dropout, retention and completion rates; regional and gender parity. The report further perceives equity as an assurance of fairness in provision of equal opportunities for all learners to access quality education irrespective of socio-economic status, geographic  location,  individual  learner  abilities,  gender  and  other  such  variables.  Equity, therefore, refers to the extent to which access provides equal opportunity for all learners.

texts.orig: From the Table, the anticipated enrolment to Secondary school in 2023 is  2,571,044 against 1,081,900 placement opportunities in 2020. This indicates a significant shortfall of 1,489,144 places  in  Secondary  schools  in  2023.  The  anticipated  enrolment  increase  will  also  require expansion of laboratories, libraries, Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) facilities and other educational  related  resources. texts.orig: 2.3.3 Funding of secondary education
texts.text: 2.3.3 Funding of secondary education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The cost of Secondary education has been identified as a challenge to access and equity globally. Education costs refer to the budget incurred by the Government and/or private sector towards education provision and are broadly categorised into two: Social costs (incurred by Government and development partners) and private costs (borne by households and corporates). Educational efficiency is  the  ability  to  fulfil  maximum  educational  potential  at  the  lowest  possible  cost (OECD, 2017). It takes into account the contexts, resources, existing synergetic relationships, complexities and diversities of educational processes to maintain quality outcomes with minimal funding, or to attain better outcomes with the same level of funding.

texts.orig: According to previous Taskforce reports, National policy documents and research studies, the cost of education is a key constraint in transition from Primary to Secondary education (NESSP, 2018).  The  main  factor  contributing  to  low  transition  and  retention  rates  to  and  through Secondary school is direct and indirect costs of education that are borne by households, especially those from low socio-economic backgrounds. texts.label: text

Though there is a preference for boarding schools, the construction of boarding facilities not only requires significant investment but also results in high recurrent costs for maintenance, thus the costs are transferred to the household (World Bank, 2008). Schools are further described by type , as either boarding or day; single gender  or  mixed  gender;  and  special  or  regular. texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Glossary of Education Reform refers to teacher capacity as the perceived abilities, skills, expertise of teachers and/or their ability to progress. Teacher capacity is critical in determining where JSS will be domiciled in the Basic Education structure. Enhancing learner achievement depends on teachers, whose performance in turn, hinges on their capacity (Todaro & Smith, 2012). This is foregrounded by, among others, review of a synthesis of more than 800 metaanalyses of 52,649 research studies (Hattie, 2009) relating to visible learning achievement. The analyses  revealed  that  the  most  important  factors  influencing  learning  achievement  are:  the teacher (35 per cent); curricula (32 per cent); and teaching (30 per cent). Other variables analysed included student, home, school and curricula. Details of the analyses are presented in Table 2.9.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Teacher  demand  is  determined  by  the  number  of  learners  enrolled;  policies  pertaining  to curriculum; subjects to be offered; prior commitments to employed teachers; funding capacity; and the stipulated wages. Teacher supply refers to the aggregate number of eligible individuals available to render services under the prevailing conditions. The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) staffing norm which is the Curriculum Based Establishment (CBE), requires a Secondary school teacher to take a minimum teaching load of 27 lessons per week and at least two subjects depending on the specialisation.  The introduction of JSS and increased learning areas in CBC pose a demand for more teachers in specialised disciplines to ensure that education quality and relevance are maintained. Further details on this are provided in Chapters three and eight.

The report further recommends that Secondary day-schooling be initiated at the JSS level and that:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: a) It  should be localised, geared towards meeting the needs of local communities whose citizens cannot afford boarding fees;

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: d) Secondary school boarding should only be considered for learners who do not have access to day schools within a reasonable distance from their homes.
texts.text: Secondary school boarding should only be considered for learners who do not have access to day schools within a reasonable distance from their homes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One  case  of  successful  implementation  of  day-schooling  is  the Neighbourhood  Attendance initiative of Shanghai, China. The policy directed that learners attend their local neighbourhood schools at Primary and JSS levels rather than compete for limited spaces at key schools . Although not well embraced initially, this initiative eventually bore positive effects including (i) bringing to an end the high-stakes in examinations occasioned by learners competing for the key schools ; (ii) indiscriminative placement in schools, leading to a more inclusive and heterogeneous learner population; and (iii) alleviation of anxiety among parents regarding placement in the schools. This experience will inform the Kenya education system during the transition period.

The Kamunge Report (GoK, 1988) also recommended establishment of day Secondary schools as a strategy for expanding access. From the foregoing discussion, it is arguable that day-schooling has multiple benefits which include reduction in education costs for households; expansion of access, especially for learners from low socio-economic status; narrowing the gender gap on access; and minimising wastage.

texts.orig: 2.4.3 Double Track as a strategy for transition
texts.text: 2.4.3 Double Track as a strategy for transition

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In some contexts, a strategy referred to as Double Track has been used to manage double intakes at various education levels, such as the one anticipated at Secondary education level in Kenya during the transition period. While this would require a well thought- out and context- specific strategy  to  avoid  creating  counterproductive  practice,  it  is  worth  understanding  its  practical relevance where resource rationalisation is critical. Double Track, also referred to as Year-Round Education  (YRE)  across  the  world,  is  an  innovative  intervention  that  allows  institutions  to accommodate increased enrolments within the same facility. This aims at reducing overcrowding and saving costs, as opposed to construction of new infrastructure for a short-term issue.

texts.text: According to the World Bank Report (2008), Double Track has been cited as one of the viable options  to  enhance  cost-effectiveness  in  Secondary  schools  and  is  also  favourable  due  to  its flexibility in timetabling. The Double Track Strategy entails:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: a) Analysis  of  the  existing  infrastructure  and  teaching  workforce  against  the  projected enrolments to identify the additional number of learners which is in excess;
texts.text: Analysis  of  the  existing  infrastructure  and  teaching  workforce  against  the  projected enrolments to identify the additional number of learners which is in excess;

texts.orig: The  Taskforce  noted  the  case  of  Ghana,  where  the  Double  -Track  system  was  successfully implemented  with  effect  from  2018/2019  during  the  implementation  of  the  policy  on  free education at Senior High School (Free SHS Programme). Following an initiative rolled out by the Government of Ghana in 2017, every learner who qualified for placement in a public Senior High School was to enjoy Government funding and as a result, the increased number of learners had to be accommodated in the existing facilities, thus stretching the recommended class sizes. The  Government  of  Ghana,  therefore,  adopted  the  Double  Track  system  alongside  other interventions, whereby selected Senior High Schools followed a Double-Track School Calendar.

Following an initiative rolled out by the Government of Ghana in 2017, every learner who qualified for placement in a public Senior High School was to enjoy Government funding and as a result, the increased number of learners had to be accommodated in the existing facilities, thus stretching the recommended class sizes. The  Government  of  Ghana,  therefore,  adopted  the  Double  Track  system  alongside  other interventions, whereby selected Senior High Schools followed a Double-Track School Calendar.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ghana Double-Track system was intended to create room, to cater for increased enrolment; reduce class sizes; and increase contact hours. The Double-Track School Calendar initiative was a  temporary stop-gap measure which was to be in place until the ideal infrastructure-learner ratios got realised. Further, it was implemented on need basis, hence not all Senior High Schools were  subjected  to  the  Double-Track  system.  Some  of  the  benefits  that  the  Ghana  education system  gained  from  adopting  a  Double-Track  system  included:  (i)  increased  contact  hours between teachers and learners, enabling teachers to have more time to complete the syllabus; (ii) optimisation of the same school infrastructure to enrol more students; (iii) avoidance or reduction of congestion in schools, leading to a reduction in class size. Moreover, the strategy was only adopted in schools where congestion was envisaged.

Lessons  from  these strategies  would  be  useful  in  implementing  the  Double  Track  system  in  the  Kenyan  Basic Education sub- sector on need basis during the 8-4-4 / 2-6-6-3 transition years.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Double-Track system is considered viable and cost effective for the transition context given that the most profound constraints on infrastructure are expected to last for two years only, hence it would not be cost effective for the Government to invest in constructing classrooms which may end up being un-utilised or under-utilised after the critical transition period. It is also important to emphasise that Double-Track can be effected on need basis, only in circumstances where there is a shortage or constraint of infrastructure.

The theories included the Child Growth and Development Theories such as: Theory of Intellectual or Cognitive Development by Jean  Piaget  (1896-1980);  Theory  of  Intellectual  Development  by  Maria  Montessori  (18701952); Psycho-sexual Theory of Development by Sigmund Freud (1856-1939); Social Learning Theory by B. F. Skinner (1904-1990); and Lev Vygotsky's Socio-cultural Theory (1896-1934). Other theoretical  and  conceptual  frameworks included the Social Learning Theory by  Albert Bandura (1977); Moral Reasoning Theory by Lawrence Kohlberg (1958); Moral Development Theory by Robert Coles (1986); Emotional Intelligence; Mixed Model of Emotional Intelligence (EI); Artificial Intelligence; and Bio-ecological Systems Theory.

These are namely: (i) the developmental stages of the learners; (ii) emotional development of learners; (iii) environmental, psychological and sociological factors; (iv) family attachment factors; and (v) the cognitive development of learners.
texts.text: Based on this, the Taskforce concluded that the child developmental stage at which transition from Primary school will occur is characterised by a complexity of interacting factors that make the following indicators crucial for consideration in determining the domiciling of JSS. These are namely: (i) the developmental stages of the learners; (ii) emotional development of learners; (iii) environmental, psychological and sociological factors; (iv) family attachment factors; and (v) the cognitive development of learners.

texts.orig: Under 8-4-4, Secondary education forms the second cycle of the education system and takes a block of four years leading to award of the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE). The 8-4-4 system has a broad curriculum in Forms 1 and 2, where learners are offered 13 subjects. However, in Forms 3 and 4 learners are allowed to select a minimum of seven and a maximum of nine subjects. Out of these, three are compulsory - Mathematics, English and Kiswahili.

The 8-4-4 system has a broad curriculum in Forms 1 and 2, where learners are offered 13 subjects. However, in Forms 3 and 4 learners are allowed to select a minimum of seven and a maximum of nine subjects. Out of these, three are compulsory - Mathematics, English and Kiswahili.

texts.orig: A comparative analysis of education structures of other African Countries and the rest of the world reveals that the Primary school cycle is shorter and focuses on numeracy and literacy, while the Secondary school cycle is longer to allow for deeper exploration of the curriculum. Secondary school is part of Basic Education, which is compulsory for all children. This conforms to  the  United  Nations'  Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs),  a  blueprint  for  global development and UNESCO's Education for All (EFA) Framework (UNESCO, 2000). Under the SDGs, Goal 4 commits Governments to provide inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all by 2030 (UNESCO, 2015).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In 2008, the Government introduced Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) that led to increased transition  of  learners  from  Primary  to  Secondary  education.  Similarly,  in  recent  years  the Government has expanded the number of Secondary schools to accommodate rising enrolments. The Economic Survey (KNBS, 2020) shows that the number of public Secondary schools rose from 8,297 in 2015 to 9,643 in 2018, representing a 16.2 per cent increase. Also, the number of private schools increased from 1,143 in 2015 to 1,756 in 2018, which is a 53.6 per cent increase. As indicated in Table 3.1, the CBC Taskforce (2020) reported that the total number of public and private Secondary schools was 10,359, representing a 7.4 per cent increase from 2018. The data also shows that public Secondary schools comprise 87.55 per cent of existing Secondary schools.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since  2017,  the  Ministry  of  Education  (MoE)  has  been  implementing  the  Kenya  Secondary Education Quality Improvement Project (SEQIP) with support from the World Bank. The sixyear project seeks to increase transition from Primary to Secondary education and, to improve learning in targeted areas that are educationally and economically marginalised and disadvantaged. Among other targeted interventions, this entails expansion of the infrastructure of 7,852 public Primary and 2,147 Secondary schools in 110 Sub-Counties across 30 Counties. Specifically, the project entails construction of 962 classrooms in 561 and 859 laboratories in 785 Secondary schools respectively.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In 2020, the MoE initiated the Elimu Scholarship Programme to improve transition to secondary education. The scheme targets to support 18,000 learners from low socio-economic backgrounds, enrolled  in  Secondary  schools  in  the  110  SEQIP  target  Sub-Counties.  In  addition,  the beneficiaries receive a social support kit, mentorship, advocacy and gender sensitisation. The pioneer cohort of 9,000 learners was awarded scholarships in 2020 and will be fully supported through the four years of Secondary education. Out of the 9,000 students selected, 4,770 (53 per cent) were females while 4,230 (47 per cent) were males. The NG-CDF also provides bursaries to learners from disadvantaged backgrounds.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Other bursary and scholarship programmes include the Jomo Kenyatta Foundation (JKF), Kenya Commercial Bank (KCB) Foundation and Equity Group Foundation (EGF). The JKF Scholarship Programme was established in 1968 to improve access and transition to Secondary education. The initiative has so far benefited more than 100,000 learners and is supported by the East Africa Philanthropic Network and Rotary Club of Nairobi Central. The KCB Foundation has also supported bright but needy learners since 200, with more than 240 beneficiaries targeted annually, some of whom have physical impairment. Similarly, the Wings to Fly Scholarship Programme  supported  by  EGF  and  Mastercard  has  provided  scholarships  to  more  than 26,000 learners since 2010. The EGF Scholarship covers school fees, transport,  learning materials, pocket money, mentorship, psychosocial support and leadership development.

texts.text: UNESCO (2000) describes quality in education as the degree to which learning and teaching meet the set standards, satisfy basic learning needs and enrich the lives of learners and their overall life experience in the process of being educated. The Dakar Framework of Action on Education for All highlights the importance of improving all aspects of quality education such as:

texts.orig: The 2009 Summative Evaluation on the 8-4-4 System of Education (KICD, 2009) established that  Secondary  education  did  not  prepare  learners  adequately  for  Tertiary  Education  and  the world of work. The system focused more on academic examinations and missed out on skills such as entrepreneurship and self-reliance (KIE, 2009).  The Odhiambo Report (GoK, 2012), NESSP (2018- 2022) and Sessional Paper No 1 of 2019 (GoK, 2019) further highlight issues that undermine quality of education, which include inadequate teachers, and insufficient teaching and learning  resources  such  as  laboratories  and  workshops.  To  address  these  quality  gaps,  the Government has embraced strategies such as provision of textbooks, instructional materials and laboratory equipment to Secondary schools (NESSP, 2018- 2022).

texts.orig: 3.3. Basic Education Curriculum Framework and its Implications
texts.text: 3.3. Basic Education Curriculum Framework and its Implications

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This section provides an overview of the BECF (KICD 2017) and its implications on transition to SSS. In the CBC, Secondary education is organised in two levels, Junior and Senior Secondary. JSS is presented in chapter two while SSS, which is the focus of this chapter, is the final level of Basic Education comprising three years and lays the foundation for further education, training and the world of work (KICD, 2017). Establishment of SSS was informed by the Odhiambo Report (MoE, 2012), which also proposed that this level should have specialisation and provide opportunities for learners to focus on areas of their interest and abilities. The report recommended that the SSS cycle have four distinct specialisation streams, namely: General, Technical, Talent and Vocational. It further stated that all SSS would follow the same core curriculum that include development of moral and values, communication skills, scientific and technological competencies. The Koech Report (GoK, 1999) had as well earlier recommended that learners be allowed to specialise in areas of their choice.

The report recommended that the SSS cycle have four distinct specialisation streams, namely: General, Technical, Talent and Vocational. It further stated that all SSS would follow the same core curriculum that include development of moral and values, communication skills, scientific and technological competencies. The Koech Report (GoK, 1999) had as well earlier recommended that learners be allowed to specialise in areas of their choice.

texts.orig: The BECF (KICD, 2017) has conceptualised SSS as a level where specialisation begins with learners making choices from a range of disciplines organised in three Pathways: Arts and Sports Science; Social Sciences; and STEM and several Tracks. The SSS Pathways and Tracks allow learners to choose an area of specialisation based on their abilities, interests and career choices. The Framework also envisages Career Guidance and Parental Empowerment and Engagement as critical in the choice of Pathways and Tracks for learners at the end of JSS.

texts.text: 3.4 Insights from International Best Practices and Stakeholder Submissions 3.4.1 Learning from best practices

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  Taskforce  reviewed  literature  from  Germany,  the  Philippines  and  Ghana,  among  other Countries  that  have  implemented  the  CBC.  It  was  found  that  in  Germany,  parents  make  the choice, based on advice from the teaching staff, whether the child should continue their school career in Junior High School, Secondary School, Grammar School, or Comprehensive School.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This choice is binding and therefore has long term implications on the child's further education and career options. In the Philippines, the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013 introduced Senior High School and this resulted in an additional two years of Secondary education, causing low enrolment in the colleges.

In the Philippines, the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013 introduced Senior High School and this resulted in an additional two years of Secondary education, causing low enrolment in the colleges.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: According  to  the  Philippines'  MoE  report,  a  number  of  higher  education  institutions  used available  infrastructure  to  offer  high  school  education.  Additionally,  more  teachers  and  nonteaching staff were hired in the subsequent two years. These were sourced from the staff at the Tertiary institutions who would otherwise have become redundant during the transition period. Therefore, nothing was lost in the infrastructure and no teacher was declared redundant. This demonstrates how rationalisation of a structure on capacity and human resource could lead to optimal utilisation of resources.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In  2017,  the  Government  of  Ghana  introduced  the  Free  Senior  High  School  policy  to  give opportunity for Primary school leavers to access Secondary education. In the first term of the 2017/2018  academic  year,  enrolment  into  the first year of Senior High  increased by approximately 63 per cent. This was achieved through the Double Track system, which made use of  the  available  but  limited  capacity  in  the  Senior  High  Schools  to  provide  educational opportunities to thousands of students. The system divided the student population and staff into two tracks. While one of the tracks attended school, the other was on vacation and vice versa. The first track was called Green track while the second is called the Gold track. To avoid teacher fatigue, arrangements were made for each track to have its own set of teaching staff.

The system divided the student population and staff into two tracks. While one of the tracks attended school, the other was on vacation and vice versa. The first track was called Green track while the second is called the Gold track. To avoid teacher fatigue, arrangements were made for each track to have its own set of teaching staff.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The benefits of the Double Track system have been cited as an increase in enrolments in schools and optimal use of school facilities, among others. However, challenges such as lack of adequate stakeholder consultation, inadequate funding, and insufficient teaching and learning materials were experienced in rollout of the Double Track system. Some teachers felt that the quality of education was compromised and there was little time to carry out maintenance of school facilities since the schools were occupied for most time of the year.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Another experience with CBC implementation is drawn from Rwanda. The Country launched CBC in 2015 although the rollout begun in 2016. The process involved creating public awareness about the new curriculum, developing the curriculum framework, training of teachers, preparing and publishing books, with emphasis on local production. The first set of national examinations under  CBC  were  administered  in  Primary  six,  Senior  three and  Senior six in 2018. Implementation of the CBC was completed within 18 months, which created pressure on schools, Government agencies and the Country at large.

Implementation of the CBC was completed within 18 months, which created pressure on schools, Government agencies and the Country at large.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Some  of  the  challenges  experienced  by  Rwanda  included  slow  publication  of  books  and development of teaching and learning materials. Despite having been trained, teachers took time to  adjust  and  shift  from  their  traditional  didactic  teaching  methods  to  interactive  ones.  Large numbers of learners in classes also created difficulty especially in the teaching of STEM and other practical subjects. Inadequate funding also affected its implementation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: From the foregoing, CBC has been widely accepted in many Countries with the SSS having been introduced with particular focus on specialisation. The respective Governments are supporting initiatives  to  develop  locally,  their  own  teaching  and  learning  materials.  Through  innovative strategies such as Double Track, it is possible to implement SSS with minimum costs. In addition, the use of local learning area networks to deliver digital learning has capacity to enhance quality and interactive learning.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Taskforce received submissions from stakeholders that highlighted various issues affecting Secondary education. These included a concern on the declining quality of Secondary education that was attributed to poor infrastructure, teacher shortage, teaching methods that encourage rote learning, and emphasis on examinations. Others were shortage of human resources in Secondary schools and the need to map out schools and to review their classification. At the same time, the stakeholders proposed that all existing Secondary schools should host SSS. In addition, each SSS should offer at least two Pathways to ensure optimal utilisation of facilities. Establishment of fully-fledged Special Needs Primary and Secondary schools was also proposed.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.1 Introduction
texts.text: 4.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter focuses on transition from Basic Education to Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET). It centres mainly on transition from Senior Secondary School (SSS) of the first Competency- based Curriculum (CBC) cohort to TVET in 2029 and the implications that this will have on the sub-sector in terms of access, relevance, transition, equity and quality. It has four main sections excluding this introduction with the first section foregrounding a situational analysis of TVET in Kenya. This focuses on access, transition equity, quality and management; and is followed by insights from international best practices and the Kenyan perspective. Finally, recommendations are presented on effective transition to TVET under the CBC reforms

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.2 Situational Analysis of the TVET Sector
texts.text: 4.2 Situational Analysis of the TVET Sector

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  section  provides  a  situational  analysis  of  the  TVET  sector.  Transition  to  TVET  is conceptualised against the provisions of the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECFKICD,  2017)  that  outlines  the  various  Pathways  and  Tracks  that  learners  will  take  at  SSS. According  to  United  Nations  Educational,  Scientific  and  Cultural  Organization  (UNESCO), Tertiary Education builds onto Secondary education, providing learning activities in specialised fields of education. This includes what is commonly understood as academic education as well as advanced vocational or professional education in middle level colleges.
texts.text: This  section  provides  a  situational  analysis  of  the  TVET  sector.  Transition  to  TVET  is conceptualised against the provisions of the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECFKICD,  2017)  that  outlines  the  various  Pathways  and  Tracks  that  learners  will  take  at  SSS. According  to  United  Nations  Educational,  Scientific  and  Cultural  Organization  (UNESCO), Tertiary Education builds onto Secondary education, providing learning activities in specialised fields of education. This includes what is commonly understood as academic education as well as advanced vocational or professional education in middle level colleges.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: UNESCO (2016) further defines TVET as those aspects of education involving the study of technologies  and  related  sciences  as  well  as  the  acquisition  of  practical  skills,  attitudes, understanding and knowledge relating to occupations in various sectors of economic life. TVET provides learners with a broad range of knowledge, skills and attitudes to enable them engage in productive occupations (UNESCO, 2016: p. 5). TVET is delivered through formal and informal programmes. The formal training comprises long-term programmes, facilitated in accordance with recognised national curricula, leading to recognized certification.

texts.orig: 4.2.2 Relevance of TVET
texts.text: 4.2.2 Relevance of TVET

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One of the main challenges for the TVET sub-sector is ability to offer relevant training that is responsive  to  market  needs  through  provision  of  skills  that  promote  sustainability  in  the workplace. There is also notable weakness in integrating entrepreneurship training, involving local  communities  and  business  communities,  not  in  the  least  increasing  responsiveness  to technological change and promoting the use of Information Communication Technologies (ICTs) as well as adapting qualifications and developing pathways to Higher Education and employment (UNESCO, 2016).  The  TVET  curricula  makes  it  mandatory  for  all  the  trainees  to  undergo industrial  attachment  before  completing  their  studies.  Further,  there  are  initiatives  to  set  up production units within TVET institutions to expose the trainees to real work experience. Despite this,  TVET  faces  various  challenges  such  as  weak  linkages  between  the  institutions  and  the industry, low level of involvement of private sector players in TVET curricula development, and minimal supervision of trainees during internships and in exchange programmes.

texts.orig: The  Odhiambo  Report  (MoE,  2012)  and  National  Education  Sector  Strategic  Plan  (NESSP, 2018-2022) call for strong links between TVET institutions and industry. Fretwell, et al. , (2001) further highlight the need for Countries to develop occupational standards to enhance industrytraining collaboration. The Big Four Agenda (MTP III, 2018-2022) prioritises the following: Universal health coverage; Food security; Affordable housing and manufacturing. Successful implementation of these require practical skills and therefore underscores the relevance of TVET programmes. This view was aptly captured in one the interviews with stakeholders.

texts.orig: The first CBC cohort (Grade 4 of 2020) will progress to Tertiary institutions in 2029. Based on the trends observed from the KCSE examination results for 2016-2019, it is estimated that about 15 per cent of 1,247,140 students from the pioneer CBC cohort (translating to 183,080 students) will  transit  to  University,  while  the  remaining  85  per  cent  (approximately 1,064,060 )  are anticipated to transit to the other Tertiary institutions. As at 2020, the placement opportunities in Tertiary institutions (excluding Universities)  could accommodate 350,000 students, leaving a deficit of about 714,060 students. This implies a need to progressively expand the infrastructure, recruit more trainers and undertake in-service training in readiness for the CBC cohort of 2029.

This  includes  tradespeople,  craftspeople, technicians,  and  high  professional  practitioner  positions  in  careers  such  as  Engineering, Accountancy, Nursing, Medicine and Architecture (GoK, 2017). Out of those who qualified, 122,831 were admitted  to  Universities  whereas  2,632  opted  for  placement  in  TVET  institutions.  In  total, 88,724, (32 per cent) of the total declared capacity of 276,163 were placed in TVET institutions. This implies that TVET institutions have capacity to accommodate more learners. texts.orig: The  Kenya  National  Qualifications  Authority  (KNQA,  2018)  developed  the  Kenya  Credit Accumulation and Transfer System (KCAT) which is the national credit transfer system for all levels of qualifications in the Country. This promotes lifelong learning and is designed for use by TVET institutions, colleges and Universities to monitor, record and reward transitions from Certificate to Diploma and Degree courses as well as to facilitate movement between levels and courses within and among institutions. Through the KCAT system, learners can gain a better understanding  of  qualifications  and  plan  their  future  learning.  The  BECF  (KICD,  2017) envisages  three  Pathways  for  the  CBC  where  students  will  have  an  opportunity  to  choose  a Pathway  that  meets  their  interest.  The  KCAT  system  will  provide  for  career  growth  and progression within the Pathways through the credit accumulation system.

texts.orig: 4.2.4 Quality in the TVET Sub-Sector
texts.text: 4.2.4 Quality in the TVET Sub-Sector

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In TVET, quality is both a process and output that is determined by the way a product is processed as it moves through the production system to its completion. Quality is also explained in two ways; technical and emotional. The technical aspect is best described by the concept of 'quality in fact' which is the conformity of an output or service to certain specifications and standards. The  emotional  aspect  is  about  the  relative  notion  of  'quality  between  bad  and  excellent' (TVETA, 2019). The quality of training in TVET is linked to occupational standards, which, in turn, are based on identified needs of the workplace and occupational profile.
texts.text: In TVET, quality is both a process and output that is determined by the way a product is processed as it moves through the production system to its completion. Quality is also explained in two ways; technical and emotional. The technical aspect is best described by the concept of 'quality in fact' which is the conformity of an output or service to certain specifications and standards. The  emotional  aspect  is  about  the  relative  notion  of  'quality  between  bad  and  excellent' (TVETA, 2019). The quality of training in TVET is linked to occupational standards, which, in turn, are based on identified needs of the workplace and occupational profile.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Occupational standards are designed to be industry-driven and depend on current as well as future needs of specific occupations. Occupational standards are the initial point of reference for the development  of  competency  based  training  programme.  Training  programme  standards  are guided  by  occupational  standards  and  form  the  basis  for  curriculum  development  (TVETA, 2019). The TVET Reform Strategy introduces a number of measures aimed at developing an attractive and inclusive TVET system. The measures aim at improving the quality of education and  training  through  appropriate  teaching  and  learning  support.  These  also  seek  to  enhance stakeholder  engagement  in  the  implementation  of  TVET.  Kenya  National  Qualifications Framework  (KNQF)  provides  criteria  for  determining  quality  and  includes  the  number  of trainers, pedagogy and resources in the respective areas of specialisation.

texts.orig: Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) is one of the criteria that will help individuals from the TVET informal sector ( Jua kali ) acquire formal qualifications that matches their knowledge and skills, and thereby contribute to improving their employability, mobility, lifelong learning, social inclusion and self-esteem. To assure quality, RPL will be assessed procedurally and equated as recommended by KNQA.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Koech Report (GoK, 1999) and the Kenya Vision 2030 (GoK, 2007) have identified various challenges  affecting  TVET  and  made  recommendations  for  enhancing  quality  training  that include: changing the poor public perception on TVET; improving learning facilities in Youth Polytechnics; ensuring quality of training services and accountability in the delivery of services; and, increasing access to TVETs through subsidy and bursaries. The Odhiambo Report (MoE, 2012) recommended a review of TVET curricula; establishment of national standards; a Quality Assurance (QA) system and retraining of QA officers, to enhance their capacity to deal with quality  and  standards  in  TVET  institutions.  The  Report  recommended  regular  upgrading  of equipment and infrastructure in the training institutions, in addition to development of in-service training for TVET trainers to upgrade their skills. Another key recommendation was that MoE reintroduces TVET subjects in the Secondary education curriculum.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Various reports have observed that there is a challenge in training of TVET trainers and managers on pedagogy and although some Universities train teachers in Technology Education, they are not able to produce enough graduates required by the sector. In view of this, most trainers and managers in TVET lack the requisite qualifications. Further, the reports also observe that linkage between  TVET  institutions  and  industry  is  weak.  A  survey  by  the  Kenya  Association  of Manufacturers (2017) established that the training content in TVET institutions did not match with  the  industry  needs.  The  report  recommended  that  TVET  trainers  undergo  industrial attachment at least every three years to upgrade their knowledge and skills and MoE implements a Framework for accreditation of TVET trainers, training providers, and assessment of trainees for QA. This was corroborated during interviews with stakeholders, who underscored the need for strong linkages between training institutions and the industry. Stakeholders also reiterated the need for TVETA to map out all TVET institutions and develop an inventory (career booklet) to guide learners on various issues including admission requirements and potential employers.

texts.orig: 4.2.5 Equity in TVET
texts.text: 4.2.5 Equity in TVET

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Equity denotes fairness in access to knowledge and skills training opportunities for learners from all  backgrounds,  including  gender,  geographical  location  and  abilities.  It  also  entails  the promotion  of  lifelong  learning  through  flexible  programmes  that  allow  every  person  to participate in continuous training and skills development. Ensuring equity requires a national skills strategy that is developed through broad participation by stakeholders.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: With the implementation of CBET, learners are exposed to different skills based on their abilities and interests. Access to TVET institutions will no longer be perceived as suitable only for those with low academic achievements but rather as a matter of choice, ability and talent. This change of  perception  was  realized  in  2019,  when  there  was  a  marked  increase  of  Secondary  school leavers opting for TVET courses even though they had attained University entry qualifications. A total of 2,632 opted for TVET institutions compared to 189 learners in 2016 (KUCCPS, 2019).

texts.text: 4.2.5.1 Gender Equity in TVET Sub- Sector

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) estimated that 43 per cent of students enrolled in vocational programmes at upper Secondary in 2017 were females, compared to 49 per cent in general education programmes. These gender disparities are more prevalent in some fields than others, with girls and women particularly under-represented in Science Technology Engineering and  Mathematics  (STEM)  at  35  per  cent  globally  (UNESCO,  2018).  The  Kenya  Economic Survey (2020) summarizes this enrolment trends as captured in Table 4.2.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: According to Table 4.2, more males than females are enrolled in TVET institutions although the enrolment was increasing generally. However, more female students tend to seek admission into private TVETs as opposed to their male counterparts who prefer the public TVETs. This could be attributed to the fact that private TVETs opt for courses such as Hospitality, Business and  Secretarial  that  are  traditionally  stereotyped  as  feminine,  while  the  public  TVETs specialize in courses such as Engineering, Technology and Medical Technology, stereotyped as masculine. This implies that more males than females access Government funding in public TVETs as the females who enrol in private TVETs do not access Government funding.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In order to attract more females into public TVETs, there is need to create awareness of the courses and break the traditional barriers that hinder women's progression into these courses. UNESCO (2018) recommends that Governments promote gender equity through legislation, policies,  quotas  and  financial  incentives  that  support  women.  This  involves  reserving scholarships and fellowships for females, to encourage more women to pursue STEM courses. Under the CBC, learners have greater opportunities to pursue TVET courses, which begin at SSS, considering that the underlying principle is interest, ability and talent. Therefore, females who show interest,  ability  and  talent  in  TVET  courses  should  be  encouraged  to  enrol  and opportunities provided for their growth.

texts.orig: 4.2.5.2 Provision of TVET to Learners with Special Needs and Disabilities
texts.text: 4.2.5.2 Provision of TVET to Learners with Special Needs and Disabilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The ILO (2017) Policy Guidelines on Inclusive TVET aim at promoting access for persons with special needs and disabilities to training opportunities as well as equipping them with knowledge  and  skills  to  enable  them  participate  in  the  labour  market  equitably.  Inclusive training  aims at ending marginalisation of people with special needs and disabilities in the labour market, and reducing social and economic costs to individuals, communities, economies and society. A national survey by the Kenya Institute of Special Education (KISE) estimated that disability prevalence among children was 11.4 per cent with a relatively even distribution of disabilities among male and female children at 51.2% and 48.8% respectively (MoE, 2018).

The MoE  advocates  for  integration  of  learners  with  special  needs  and  disabilities  in  regular educational institutions and has established four TTIs for this purpose. These are Machakos TTI for the Blind, Karen TTI for the Deaf, Sikri TTI for the Deaf and Blind, and Nyang'oma TTI for the Deaf, which by 2020 had enrolled nearly 2,500 learners, as shown in Table 4.3.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.2.6 Financing of Technical, Vocational Education and Training
texts.text: 4.2.6 Financing of Technical, Vocational Education and Training

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Medium Term Plan (MTP) III (2018-2022) highlights Vocational and Technical Training programmes and projects to be implemented during the period to address interventions and recommendations made under the sector priority areas for achievement of the training goals outlined in the Kenya Vision 2030 . This commits to ensure adequate funding to enable TVET students  participate  fully  and  complete  their  education  and  training  as  scheduled  in  the respective  programmes.  The  project  entails:  developing  a  policy  framework  for  student financing  so  that  TVET  trainees  are  funded  on  a  Differentiated  Unit  Cost  (DUC)  model; enhancement  of  student  loans  and  bursaries; establishment  of a targeted scholarship programme in STEM; and creation of a fund for financing TVET trainees. This resonates well with stakeholders' sentiments which  underscored the need to  ' Increase funding for polytechnics, institutes of technology and middle-level colleges.. . (KICD, 2020).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.2.7 Innovations and Incubations
texts.text: 4.2.7 Innovations and Incubations

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) Policy (MoE, 2017) mandates the MoE in collaboration with TVETA and other stakeholders with the responsibility of mainstreaming ESD and Green  Economy principles  and  practices  into  TVET  systems.  The  strategy  is  to introduce incubators in TVET and to encourage entrepreneurship for the youth. This can be achieved  through deliberate  efforts  of  sourcing  local  and  international  experts  through institutional  collaborations  and  tasking  them  to  develop  specific  products  for  the  industry; thereafter incubating the products into the local market, followed by their commercialisation. The STEM pathway in the BECF (KICD, 2017) provides the opportunity for innovation and incubation to thrive. More specifically, CBET should focus on the development of new and innovative products for the industry such as solar cars, green energy and blue economy.

texts.orig: 4.2.8.1 Regulatory, Certification and Staffing of TVET
texts.text: 4.2.8.1 Regulatory, Certification and Staffing of TVET

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Several agencies are involved in regulation, curriculum development and assessment of TVET. These are TVETA, TVET CDACC, KNQA, Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC), Kenya  Institute  of  Curriculum  Development  (KICD),  Kenya  Accountants  and  Secretaries National Examination Board (KASNEB) and Commission for University Education (CUE). In addition, there are multiple policies and legislation that guide TVET mainly because TVET institutions are spread across different Ministries thus creating challenges in the governance of TVET. The Economic Survey (2019) indicates that some TVET institutions are run by different structures  such  as  Management  Committees,  Boards  of  Management  (BoM),  Boards  of Trustees, and Boards of Directors, hence raises questions about the governance of TVET.

texts.text: 4.2.8.2 Coordination between National and County Governments on TVET

texts.orig: The National Government, through the Directorate of Youth Training (DYT), is responsible for developing the National Policy for Youth Polytechnics and the Vocational sector. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.3.2 Dual Certification
texts.text: 4.3.2 Dual Certification

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dual certification entails a combination of theory and training embedded in a real-life work environment. It has gained popularity in Germany, which has created dual training system that is highly recognised worldwide. Trainees in the dual system spend some days of the week at a Vocational  school  and  a  company,  or  they  may  spend  longer  periods  at  each  place  before alternating.  Dual  training  usually  lasts  two  to  three-and-a-half  years  with  the  industry participating in training and testing. In addition, certificates are standardised in all industries throughout  the  Country  (UNESCO-UNEVOC,  2015).  In  Australia,  there  is  the  option  to undertake qualifications at school, in the workplace or in registered training institutions. This has streamlined TVET training and enhanced the role of the public, private, community and industry in skills development.

A dual certification programme will enhance career opportunities for students depending  on  their  abilities  and  interests.  This  will  be  accomplished  through  partnerships between schools, Tertiary institutions and business, industry or employers. Dual certification is intended to (a) increase learner retention and completion rates (b) enhance participation of young  adults  in  post-  Secondary  programmes  (c)  assist  young  adults  to  make  meaningful connections to current and emerging labour markets and finally (d) expand local partnerships to offer dual certification programmes and internships. Dual certification is envisaged to enable learners enrol in Vocational or Technical institutions to pursue their specialisations, or join the world of work and practice under the supervision of skilled and experienced personnel.

texts.orig: 4.3.4 Transition from Senior Secondary to Tertiary
texts.text: 4.3.4 Transition from Senior Secondary to Tertiary

texts.label: text
texts.orig: UNESCO (2016) recommended that  Governments  should  develop  Pathways  and  facilitate transitions  between  Secondary,  post-  Secondary  and  Tertiary  Education,  including  flexible admission procedures and guidance; credit accumulation and transfer; bridging programmes; and, equivalency schemes that are recognised and accredited by relevant authorities. Therefore, developing  TVET  programmes  as  a  Pathway  to  lifelong  learning,  which  includes  Higher Education is a priority for the educational reforms, consistent with  the  UNESCO recommendations.

texts.text: 4.3.5 TVET Curriculum Harmonisation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The East African Community called upon TVET authorities from the region to harmonise curriculum  (EAC,  2014).  The  harmonisation  is  supported  by  the  East  Africa  Skills  for Transformation and Regional Integration Project (EASTRIP) which aims at promoting regional integration  and  improving  the  quality  of  TVET  programmes  among  Member  States. Harmonisation of skills through the curriculum targets critical sectors such as Manufacturing, Transport, Energy, ICT and the Blue Economy. Also targeted is harmonisation of examinations and qualifications across the region, which will facilitate the mobility of TVET graduates.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.3.6 Perception of TVET
texts.text: 4.3.6 Perception of TVET

texts.label: text
texts.orig: UNESCO (2018) observes that the negative perception about TVET in many Countries has led to  low  uptake  of  the  programmes  and  subsequent  shortage  of  skilled  workers  to  meet  the requirements of enterprises and to serve national development needs. In this context, UNESCO proposes strategies for changing the image of TVET. These include; making TVET a core Pathway in education programmes and mounting public campaigns to sensitise young people, parents,  employers  and  educators  about  its  potential.  Since  2015,  UNESCO  has  been supporting TVET programmes among Member States through policy advice, capacity-building and  policy  reviews  to  improve  quality  and  relevance.  UNESCO's  campaign  is  to  position TVET as a viable learning Pathway that contributes to equity, social justice, lifelong learning and sustainable development .

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.1 Introduction
texts.text: 5.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter addresses transition from Senior Secondary School (SSS) to University Education in 2029 with a focus on infrastructure and human resource requirements and their implication on access, relevance, transition, equity and quality. It is organised into four main sections that include  this  introduction,  the  role  and  contexts,  followed  by  situational  analysis  and recommendations.  The  2-6-6-3  structural  reforms  in  the  context  of  the  Competency  based Curriculum (CBC) implies that University Education courses will take a minimum of three years.  The  transition  to  University  Education  is  considered  against  the  background  of  the provisions in the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECF- KICD, 2017) that highlights the various Pathways learners will take at SSS. Also considered is the Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019 (GoK, 2019) that recommends aligning University to the Pathways offered at SSS.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.2 Role and Context of University Education
texts.text: 5.2 Role and Context of University Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Globally, University Education plays a critical role in the socio-economic development of any nation. This is achieved through research and quality training and development of a skilled workforce that matches the unique developmental needs of a given Country. In Kenya, the central  role  of  Universities  in  realisation  of  national  development  has  been  emphasized  in several policy documents including the Kenya Vision 2030 and Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019. This is further stressed by the Taskforce on the Realignment of the Education Sector to the Constitution  of  Kenya  2010  (Odhiambo  Report,  2012),  and  the  Big  Four  Agenda  of  2018 (MTP-III, 2018-2022). In all these, Universities are seen as providing a critical mass of skilled human resource to drive the various sectors and are therefore expected to conduct research to provide solutions to the problems faced by the Country.

texts.orig: Such  developments  necessitate  a  University  system  with  a  sound  tradition  of  Science, Technology and Innovation that is key to the creation of a sustainable pool of highly skilled human resource base.
