texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 5.3 Situational Analysis on University Education in Kenya
texts.text: 5.3 Situational Analysis on University Education in Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  section  provides  a  situational  analysis  of  University  Education  in  Kenya,  under  five themes of access, relevance, transition, equity and quality. Based on the situational analysis, a set of recommendations is given with a rationale on each issue. This is based on insights from relevant  literature,  international  best  practices,  stakeholder  engagements  and  primary  data obtained from the field. Further, the section provides suggestions on policy, legal provisions and strategies for effective implementation of the recommendations including implementation logistics, work plans, responsible organisations, and cost implications.

texts.text: 5.3.1 Access to University Education in Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  University  sub-sector  in  Kenya  has  expanded  rapidly  over  the  past  three  decades.  At present, Kenya's University Education sector comprises 74 institutions; making it one of the largest Higher Education systems in Africa. The Country has 31 Chartered public Universities, six  public  Constituent  Colleges,  19  Chartered  private  Universities,  five  private  University Constituent Colleges and 13 Universities with Letters of Interim Authority. Besides these, there are four institutions approved  for  collaboration with Universities in  offering  Degree programmes. This is summarized in Table 5.1.

texts.orig: Since 2016/17, all candidates with Grade C+ and above were admitted to public Universities. However, not all the admitted students took up the places in public Universities, with some preferring to join private Universities, pursue further studies abroad or enroll for programmes in  Technical  Vocational  Education  and  Training  (TVET)  or  other  Tertiary  institutions. Nonetheless, public Universities admit the largest number of students who are attracted by affordability.  Enrolments  in  private  Universities  have  been  augmented  by  the  policy  that allowed admission of Government-sponsored students to private Universities. These developments  and  trends  provide  sufficient  evidence  that  there  are  many  opportunities  for University Education in Kenya.

texts.orig: According  to  the  Kenya  University  and  Colleges  Central  Placement  Services  (KUCCPS) shows  that  approximately  122,000  students  enrol  in  the  University  every  year  (KUCCPS, 2020).  By  2020,  the  total  University  enrolments  stood  at  510,000  and  using  the  current enrolment of 1.247 million Grade 4 learners, it is projected that about 420,000 students will join University in 2029. This assumes that 33 per cent of the students will transit to University while the remaining 67 per cent join various Tertiary institutions. It is further projected that in the next nine years, University enrolments will increase three-fold, adding up to a total of about 1.2  million.  Given  this  scenario,  it  is  important  that  the  infrastructure  of  Universities  be addressed and additional resources allocated to mitigate any possible challenges.

texts.orig: The KUCCPS is mandated with placement of post-Secondary graduates in Higher Education institutions. Under the 8-4-4 system, University placement applies to students who obtain a Grade  C+  and  above  in  the  KCSE  and  is  based  on  capacities  declared  by  individual Universities.  Since  the  placed  students  are  eligible  for  Government  sponsorship,  capitation funding to Universities is  based on the number of students placed by KUCCPS.  Table 5.5 shows that almost all the students (99 per cent) who qualified were placed in Universities.

texts.orig: Kenya Vision 2030 places great emphasis on the link between education and the labour market; the  need  to  inculcate  entrepreneurial  skills  and  competences  in  the  learners;  as  well  as,  to strengthen  partnerships  with  the  private  sector. texts.orig: Reflections on reorienting curricula to labour market needs also featured in the Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2005 (GoK, 2005), which recommended provision of opportunities that link TVET programmes with those offered in Universities. The Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019  further recommended alignment  of  existing  curricula  to  the  requirements  of  the  labour  market.  It postulates that the broad engineering profession is typically considered to comprise four cadres of  staff,  namely:  engineer,  technologist,  technician  and  crafts  and  artisan  persons.  The Sessional  Paper  notes  that  for  effective  execution  of  the  engineering  function  within  an economy, it is important that each of these cadres is represented in appropriate proportions. For most developed Countries the ideal ratios for the four categories is 1:3:12:60.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: KUCCPS places students into Universities based on the declared spaces in the different courses by the Universities. However, there are no mechanisms for KUCCPS to verify if the declared capacities are based on availability of University facilities and teaching staff. Universities can enhance  their  capacities  by  increasing  virtual  space  for  online  courses  that  would  allow admission of fee-paying but non-resident students outside the KUCCPS admissions system in line with laid down CUE regulations.

Data  from  chartered  public  and private  Universities  showed  that  majority  of  students  enrolled  in  both  public  and  private Universities originated from Nairobi County (9.56 per cent) followed by Kisii (5.20 per cent) and Kiambu (4.68 per cent) Counties. texts.orig: 5.3.4.4. Affirmative Action for Persons from Marginalised Areas
texts.text: 5.3.4.4. Affirmative Action for Persons from Marginalised Areas

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To address the inequalities,  Universities  have  been  implementing  an  affirmative  action  for persons from marginalised areas. This entails admission to University at five points below the general cut off points for students from Counties classified by the Commission on Revenue Allocation as marginalised. These include Turkana, Garissa, Marsabit, Tana River, Mandera, Lamu, Wajir, Taita Taveta, Isiolo, Kwale, Samburu, Kilifi, West Pokot and Narok. Under this intervention, female students are admitted to University with two points lower than their male counterparts.  Female  and  male  students  are  also  selected  into  specific  programmes  with  a maximum of two points lower, subject  to  attainment  of  one-third  gender  representation  in programmes that are either male or female dominated.

Female  and  male  students  are  also  selected  into  specific  programmes  with  a maximum of two points lower, subject  to  attainment  of  one-third  gender  representation  in programmes that are either male or female dominated.

texts.orig: 5.3.4.5. Student Loan Financing
texts.text: 5.3.4.5. Student Loan Financing

texts.label: text
texts.orig: HELB was established through an Act of Parliament to manage financial assistance to students enrolled in Kenyan public and private Universities and TVET institutions. This was intended to address the inequalities occasioned by gender, regional and socio-cultural disparities. HELB awards two sets of loans; one for fresh Secondary school graduates and another for salaried students. The former is targeted at students admitted to public or private Universities within the  East  African  Community  (EAC).  These  are  identified  following  their  graduation  from Secondary school through the KUCCPS or as self-sponsored students. Loans dispensed range from a minimum of KES. 35,000 to a maximum of KES. 60,000, according to the student's need. The loans are subject to an interest rate of 4 per cent per annum and students are required to commence repayment on completion of their studies.

Quality  of  academic  programmes includes  adherence  to  set  standards,  public  accountability  and  fitness  for  purpose. texts.orig: Staffing in Universities plays a critical role in the delivery of academic programmes. Available data indicates that Kenyan Universities rely considerably on part-time services and some of the staff are not qualified to teach academic programmes as per the CUE guidelines (Audit Report, CUE, 2017).  Lecturers with Masters Degree may teach undergraduate programmes as tutorial fellows while those with undergraduate qualifications are often engaged as Graduate Assistants or support staff. However, Table 5.8 shows that only about 30% of the University academic staff have PhD qualifications, which is the requisite to teach at University level.

texts.orig: 5.3.5.2 Infrastructure
texts.text: 5.3.5.2 Infrastructure

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It  is  globally  agreed  that  physical  facilities  are  critical  in  achieving  an  all-inclusive  and sustainable  quality  University  Education.  The  University  Standards  and  Guidelines,  (CUE, 2014) outline the minimum standards for infrastructure that support academic programmes as well as additional mandatory physical facilities such as workshops, studios and laboratories required in different academic disciplines. These further require that University programmes be supported by up-to-date, relevant and adequate facilities and equipment in addition to wellresourced libraries for quality teaching, learning and research. Public Universities collectively host more than 80 per cent of all students enrolled in Universities in the Country (CUE, 2017) which is beyond their established capacity. Inadequate teaching space could affect the quality of  teaching  and  learning  unless  mitigating  steps  are  instituted  focusing  on  expansion  of University infrastructure, in preparation for the CBC.

texts.orig: 6.1 Introduction
texts.text: 6.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter addresses issues pertaining to access, relevance, transition, equity and quality for learners with special needs and disabilities in the curriculum reforms. Learners with special needs include those who are Gifted and Talented as they have special needs that require special attention to ensure they remain included in the process of education. All the Taskforce Terms of Reference (ToR) have implications, explicitly or implicitly, on education for learners with special needs and disabilities, thus dictating the need to isolate and address the pertinent issues comprehensively.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter begins by expounding the meaning of key concepts in Special Needs Education (SNE). This is followed by a situational analysis of SNE focusing on the policy  and legal landscape, the current status of SNE at various education levels, and support for SNE through financial and human resources. The key issues in SNE that bear considerable impact on its implementation  are  discussed.  These  are  mainly  linked  to  policy  and  legal  contexts, governance,  resource  allocation,  access,  transition,  relevance  of  SNE,  quality  and  equity. Finally, the chapter presents recommendations for addressing these issues in order to inform ways and means of enhancing access, equity, quality, transition and relevance in SNE.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 6.2 Key Concepts in Special Needs Education (SNE)
texts.text: 6.2 Key Concepts in Special Needs Education (SNE)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  section  elucidates  key  concepts  in  SNE  as  used  in  the  Basic  Education  Curriculum Framework (BECF; KICD, 2017).
texts.text: This  section  elucidates  key  concepts  in  SNE  as  used  in  the  Basic  Education  Curriculum Framework (BECF; KICD, 2017).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: According  to  United  Nations  Scientific  and  Cultural  Organization  (UNESCO),  SNE  is designed to facilitate learning by individuals who, for a variety of reasons, require additional support and adaptive pedagogical methods to participate and achieve the expected learning outcomes. Such education programmes may follow the regular curriculum while providing specific resources (such as specially trained teaching and assistive personnel, equipment or space)  and,  if  appropriate,  modified  educational  content  that  entails  customised  expected learning outcomes. These programmes can be offered to individual learners within alreadyexisting  education  programmes  or  as  a  separate  class  in  the  same  or  separate  educational institutions (UNESCO Institute of Statistics, 2012). The BECF provides for a SNE Model that takes  care  of  four  aspects:  adapted,  accelerated,  enriched,  specialised  curriculum,  and intervention programmes.
texts.text: According  to  United  Nations  Scientific  and  Cultural  Organization  (UNESCO),  SNE  is designed to facilitate learning by individuals who, for a variety of reasons, require additional support and adaptive pedagogical methods to participate and achieve the expected learning outcomes. Such education programmes may follow the regular curriculum while providing specific resources (such as specially trained teaching and assistive personnel, equipment or space)  and,  if  appropriate,  modified  educational  content  that  entails  customised  expected learning outcomes. These programmes can be offered to individual learners within alreadyexisting  education  programmes  or  as  a  separate  class  in  the  same  or  separate  educational institutions (UNESCO Institute of Statistics, 2012). The BECF provides for a SNE Model that takes  care  of  four  aspects:  adapted,  accelerated,  enriched,  specialised  curriculum,  and intervention programmes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Inclusive  education  entails  ensuring  that  all  learning  institutions  accommodate  all  learners regardless  of  their  social  and  cognitive  capabilities,  needs,  desires  and  learning  styles.  It involves provision of reasonable accommodations characterised by flexibility, responsiveness and  support  (BECF;  KICD,  2018).  This  is  well  in  line  with  UNESCO's  (2009)  view  on inclusive education. Curriculum adaptation entails adjusting the existing curriculum to meet the  diverse  needs  of  learners  with  special  needs  in  areas  that  cannot  be  accessed  despite utilization  of  assistive  aids  and  additional  learning  materials.  Adaptations  may  include  the modification or substitution of curriculum content or learning outcomes, and modification of strategies, resources and assessment.

It involves provision of reasonable accommodations characterised by flexibility, responsiveness and  support  (BECF;  KICD,  2018). Curriculum adaptation entails adjusting the existing curriculum to meet the  diverse  needs  of  learners  with  special  needs  in  areas  that  cannot  be  accessed  despite utilization  of  assistive  aids  and  additional  learning  materials.  Adaptations  may  include  the modification or substitution of curriculum content or learning outcomes, and modification of strategies, resources and assessment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Accelerated and enriched curriculum is intended to provide the Gifted and Talented learners with  opportunities  to  realise  their  full  potential.  According  to  the  International  Bureau  of Education (IBE, 2013), Gifted and Talented learners are those whose potential is distinctly above average in one or more of four domains: intellectual, creative, social and physical. The BECF  (KICD,  2017)  provides  for  two  accommodations  for  Gifted  and  Talented  learners: differentiation and acceleration. Differentiation involves enrichment of content by providing additional  or  advanced  content,  resources  and  assessment. Acceleration allows  a  learner  to progress through school at a faster than usual rate and/or younger than typical age, through either subject acceleration, grade acceleration, early entry, telescoping or radical acceleration.

The BECF  (KICD,  2017)  provides  for  two  accommodations  for  Gifted  and  Talented  learners: differentiation and acceleration. Differentiation involves enrichment of content by providing additional  or  advanced  content,  resources  and  assessment. Acceleration allows  a  learner  to progress through school at a faster than usual rate and/or younger than typical age, through either subject acceleration, grade acceleration, early entry, telescoping or radical acceleration.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Specialised curriculum in is conceptualised as stage-based to meet the unique needs of learners with special educational needs and disabilities, who may not follow the regular curriculum (BECF; KICD, 2017). The specialised curriculum focuses on daily living skills, basic academic and work related skills for independent living. This curriculum is organised into four levels: Foundation, Intermediate, Pre-vocational and Vocational. UNESCO'S IBE provides that this kind of curriculum should be age and developmentally appropriate, taking into account specific challenges  and  contributing  to  full  development  of  the  learner's  potential.  This  is  realised through Individualised Education Plans (IEPs). Learners who are exceptionally talented and gifted would require personalised curricula that accommodates accelerated learning.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Lastly,  intervention  programmes  are  those  developed  to  guide  the  teachers,  parents  and caregivers in providing appropriate training and care for learners with profound disabilities. These  learners  are  usually  homebound,  bed-ridden  or  hospitalised  and  mostly  under unqualified caregivers or unskilled parents (BECF; KICD, 2017). Support for such learners should be organized to include Individualised Family Support Plan (IFSP) and the IEP.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Taskforce noted that significant gains have been realised in the formulation of legal and policy  frameworks to  facilitate  effective  provision  of  SNE.  Since  independence,  following recommendations of Education Commissions and Taskforces, the Government has consistently developed policy and legislation to support education for learners and trainees with special needs and disabilities. The Taskforce highlights selected chronological milestones that have been achieved since independence.

Since  independence,  following recommendations of Education Commissions and Taskforces, the Government has consistently developed policy and legislation to support education for learners and trainees with special needs and disabilities. The Taskforce highlights selected chronological milestones that have been achieved since independence.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ngala Mwendwa Committee on Care and Rehabilitation of the Disabled (GoK, 1964) informed the Sessional Paper No. 5 of 1965 that emphasised the care and rehabilitation of Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) in Kenya. Recommendations of the Ominde Commission (GoK, 1964a) yielded to greater focus on teacher training for special education, as well as the integration of learners with mild and moderate disabilities in the regular schools.
texts.text: The Ngala Mwendwa Committee on Care and Rehabilitation of the Disabled (GoK, 1964) informed the Sessional Paper No. 5 of 1965 that emphasised the care and rehabilitation of Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) in Kenya. Recommendations of the Ominde Commission (GoK, 1964a) yielded to greater focus on teacher training for special education, as well as the integration of learners with mild and moderate disabilities in the regular schools.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  Gachathi  Report  (GoK  1976)  led  to  establishment  of  Pre-primary  classes  in  special schools, and Education Assessment Resource Centres (EARCs). The Kamunge Report (GoK, 1988) recommended that SNE inspectors (currently referred to as Quality Assurance Officers) be  deployed  at  the  district  level  (now  Sub-County)  level.  Recommendations  of  the  Koech Commission (GoK, 1999) led to development of the SNE Policy and abolishment of school ranking.  The  Kochung  Report  (MoE,  2003)  guided  the  management  of  SNE,  training  of teachers on special and inclusive education, development of appropriate curricula and related services. texts.orig: The 2018 Sector Policy for Learners and Trainees with Disabilities further identifies various challenges for learners with disabilities. texts.orig: The 2019 National Census established that 2.2 per cent of Kenyans aged five years and above have a special need or disability, translating to 918,270 Kenyans (KNBS, 2020). The census considered a limited range of special needs, but this is the lowest estimation ever established by any study. Other available estimates of the disability prevalence include the Kenya Institute of Special Needs (KISE) National Survey (2018), which reported 11.4 per cent prevalence, based on 3-21 years; the 2009 Kenya National Census which reported 3.5 per cent; and, the Kenya National Survey for Persons with Disabilities (2006) which reported 4.6 per cent.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Using these results, the population of Kenyans with special needs and disabilities may vary from 400,000 to 2.3 million. Though this is not documented anywhere, one could attribute the sharp variations to lack of standardised methodology and tools of inquiry into disability, the varying range of categories included in the various studies, varying age brackets, as well as different  capacities  (specialist  and  non-specialist)  of  the  researchers  and  enumerators  who conducted the studies. Despite the variations, the estimates indicate that a higher proportion of PWDs live in the rural areas, and that there is near gender parity in the proportions of PWDs and special needs across the Kenyan population. Notwithstanding this, there exists a gap in the data of the proportion of Kenyan children whose special needs are based on their exceptionally high giftedness or talent and who require special education interventions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Taskforce Survey of 2020 also revealed that out of the 179,320 SNE learners in Primary schools,  26,288  are  in  Special  Primary  schools,  while  153,032  are  in  the  regular  Primary schools. Only 5,718 learners with special needs and disabilities transit to regular Secondary schools, while 3,895 transit to Special Secondary schools. The study further revealed that 72.6 per cent of children with disabilities are in rural and urban informal settlements. These areas have  few  or  no  special  schools,  but  boast  of  an  increase  in  the  number  of  day  Secondary schools.  Clearly,  the  accommodation  of  learners  with  disabilities  and  special  needs  in  the regular schools is indicative of the existing potential for inclusion and resource optimisation if well planned. This will enable the Government release resources for addressing the evidently low transition rates of SNE learners in order to realize the 100 per cent transition policy.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Historically, the relevance of SNE has been a long-standing issue. The NESSP (MoE, 20182022)  enlisted  challenges  such  as  inadequate  relevant  teaching  and  learning  resources  and technology for learners and trainees with disabilities; use of Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) as the medium of instruction for learners with hearing disabilities; lack of institutionalised PreVocational training opportunities; lack of exit strategies from the SNE system; and, use of outdated  technologies  in  teaching  and  learning.  To  address  these  challenges,  the  Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) has provided curriculum designs for the different categories of learners with special needs to ensure that their needs are met.
texts.text: Historically, the relevance of SNE has been a long-standing issue. The NESSP (MoE, 20182022)  enlisted  challenges  such  as  inadequate  relevant  teaching  and  learning  resources  and technology for learners and trainees with disabilities; use of Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) as the medium of instruction for learners with hearing disabilities; lack of institutionalised PreVocational training opportunities; lack of exit strategies from the SNE system; and, use of outdated  technologies  in  teaching  and  learning.  To  address  these  challenges,  the  Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) has provided curriculum designs for the different categories of learners with special needs to ensure that their needs are met.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The BECF (KICD, 2017) focuses on learner competencies within their levels of ability. To achieve this, it provides for an Age-based Curriculum for regular learners, with three different pathways in Senior Secondary School (SSS) that accommodate learners with varied abilities namely: Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Social Sciences, Arts and Sports. Moreover, learners with severe and profound disabilities who may not pursue the Agebased Curriculum have a separate stage-based curriculum.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The BECF (KICD, 2017) therefore provides for a curriculum for SNE learners within the Basic Education structure that begins at Foundational level, moves through the Intermediate level and the Pre-Vocational level to the Vocational skills level as shown in Figure 6.1. Accordingly, transition at various levels of the Stage-based Pathways will be informed by the achievement of the set learning outcomes. Continuous assessment to inform and improve learning will play a critical role in the learning process

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Though the promise of inclusive education has been articulated in various policies over the past decade, the general Teacher Education (TE) curriculum has so far not included any training on inclusion. Since 1986, the training of Primary school teachers has been limited to the inservice  certificate  and  diploma  courses  offered  at  the  Kenya  Institute  of  Special  Education (KISE). The less than 30,000 teachers that KISE has so far trained, may not lead Kenya to attain the dream of inclusive education. To address this, the MoE undertook to reform TE by first aligning teacher training to the demands of the new curriculum, and secondly, entrenching basic training on inclusion in all Pre-service Teacher Education (PTE) courses.

To address this, the MoE undertook to reform TE by first aligning teacher training to the demands of the new curriculum, and secondly, entrenching basic training on inclusion in all Pre-service Teacher Education (PTE) courses.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The reformed PTE curriculum requires all teacher trainees to study inclusive education as part of the core curriculum. The trainees will be provided with basic skills on special needs and disabilities to enhance their knowledge and practice. With regard to capacity development, the Teachers' Service Commission (TSC) has made provisions for a separate in-service training for teachers of learners with special needs and disabilities in order to allow adequate attention to SNE issues. To ensure quality, this training is facilitated by SNE specialists.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: However, various studies have established that most of the existing EARCs lack the equipment, infrastructure and human resource to provide quality and timely assessment and placement services. For instance, the 2018 KISE Survey established that while 77 per cent of the boys and 68 per cent of the girls in the Special Primary schools had been assessed prior to admission, only 43 per cent of the boys and 35 per cent of the girls in the integrated Primary schools had been assessed. The study also established that most EARCs were using multidisciplinary teams to  assess  learners,  including  physiotherapists and occupational therapists among others and there were notable shortages of speech therapists and nutritionists.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Further, most of the EARC officers (86 per cent) were specialised in only five areas - Hearing Impairment  Visual  Impairment,  Physical  Impairment,  Mental  Handicaps  and  inclusive education. Hardly any officers had specialisation in assessment of persons who are Gifted and Talented or the Deaf-blind. Subsequently, a majority of the learners assessed in 2015/16 (71 per  cent)  were  in  the  four  mentioned  disabilities,  while  only  1  per  cent  were  assessed  for giftedness. Even though health is a devolved function, 77 per cent of the officers confirmed the lack of support from County Governments.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  Taskforce  noted  that  the  Government  had  completed  construction  of  an  ultra-modern assessment and resource centre at KISE, which was in the process of being furnished through a public-private partnership. The Government had further identified ten regional EARCs that would benefit from a collaboration with partners to enhance their capacity. However, the lack of a clear link between KISE and the EARCs, coupled with lack of clear referral mechanisms for complicated special needs cases continues to pose challenges in the governance structure, for ensuring that this massive Government investment strengthens the capacities of the EARCs Countrywide. It was also noted that the assessment tools currently in use by the EARCs were developed over two decades ago, hence outdated. These were also insufficient and unsuitable for emerging spectrum of special needs and disabilities in education.

texts.orig: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in SNE
texts.text: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in SNE

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Sector Policy for Learners and Trainees with Disabilities (MoE, 2018) notes that SNE should  seek  to  prepare  the  learners  and  trainees  with  disabilities  to  function  competitively within a highly integrated, technologically oriented information-based global economy. Kildal (2008) argues that Information Communication Technology (ICT) can contribute significantly in ensuring that learners with disabilities access quality inclusive education. Integration of ICT and  assistive  technology  potentially  enhances  effectiveness  of  teaching  and  learning  for learners with special needs and disabilities and boosts the development of life skills.

Kildal (2008) argues that Information Communication Technology (ICT) can contribute significantly in ensuring that learners with disabilities access quality inclusive education. Integration of ICT and  assistive  technology  potentially  enhances  effectiveness  of  teaching  and  learning  for learners with special needs and disabilities and boosts the development of life skills.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: KISE has set up three ICT labs with capacity of about 90 users to prepare teachers for ICT integration (KISE, 2020). However, the perception is that most of teachers in SNE institutions do  not  integrate  ICT  in  their  teaching  and  learning  and  that,  generally,  the  level  of  ICT integration in SNE remains rather low. It is noteworthy that KICD has developed and executed a  Framework  for  developing  digital  content  and  providing  access  to  online  platforms,  and enhanced  coverage  of interactive radio and television lessons. Also, the Centre for Mathematics,  Science  and  Technology  in  Africa  (CEMASTEA),  which  retools  Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) teachers through ICT, was  yet to  fully integrate SNE, thus revealing a gap in the provision of SNE.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  Taskforce  confirmed  that  the  Government  had  set  aside  two  institutions  to  produce learning materials and equipment for SNE; KISE and the Kenya Institute of the Blind (KIB). However, SNE schools were  still  not  well  resourced  for  the  quality  of  services  they  were expected to offer. While traditional devices like wheelchairs, clutches, braille machines and white canes were more available, more expensive and modern equipment such as embossers, head pointers and mouth sticks were hard to come by.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  evidence  corroborates  the  2018  KISE  survey  which  provides  evidence  of  the  poor infrastructure and inadequacy of equipment for SNE learning and training. For instance, of the 124 schools that had learners with Hearing Impairments, only 10 per cent of them had either a speech room or a speech training unit. Similarly, only 8 per cent of the schools with autistic learners  had  access  to  therapists,  while  only  2  per  cent  had  study  carrels.  Access  to Physiotherapy for learners with physical disabilities was only confirmed for 32 per cent of the schools, while only 17 per cent of the schools had hand rails to support movement; only 23 per cent of schools with learners with Visual Impairments had adapted geometry kits, and only 33 per cent of the Deaf-blind had access to qualified orientation and mobility instructors.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Equity in education is a measure of achievement, fairness and opportunity. It is dependent on two main factors: fairness which implies that factors specific to one personal condition should not  interfere  with  one's  potential  of  academic  access,  and  inclusion  which  refers  to  a comprehensive standard which applies to everyone in the education system.

The differentiated ratios in favour of the males imply that the policy of inclusivity was not being applied in the regular TVET institutions.

texts.orig: 6.4 Summary of the issues and challenges in Special Needs Education
texts.text: 6.4 Summary of the issues and challenges in Special Needs Education

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 6.4.1 Policy and Governance issues
texts.text: 6.4.1 Policy and Governance issues

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. Lack of a comprehensive inclusive education policy:  Even though the Sector Policy for Learners and Trainees with Disabilities (MoE, 2018) and the Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019 claim a basis on inclusive education, the Country needs an explicit Inclusive Education policy to guide the progressive movement towards inclusion.
texts.text: Lack of a comprehensive inclusive education policy:  Even though the Sector Policy for Learners and Trainees with Disabilities (MoE, 2018) and the Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019 claim a basis on inclusive education, the Country needs an explicit Inclusive Education policy to guide the progressive movement towards inclusion.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Inadequate legal provisions:  The recommendations of Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019 are hinged on revision of the Basic Education Act (2013), including the restructuring of KISE; differentiated funding; standardisation of assessment tools; enhanced funding for  EARCs;  and  strengthening  the  use  of  multi-disciplinary  teams  in  functional assessment. However, these issues were not captured in the amendments of the Basic Education Act (2013).

However, these issues were not captured in the amendments of the Basic Education Act (2013).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iii. Lack of a centralised data set on SNE: SNE data is scattered, and varies greatly across the  various  studies.  The  available  data  is  far  too  inadequate  for  effective  decision making. For instance, it is not clear whether the Registrar of Births captures babies born with disabilities. Even then, such data is not available to the education sector, and may also  not  be  available  at  the  Ministry  of  Health.  The  current  National  Education Management Information System (NEMIS) is a stand-alone spot of data, which also misses on various key variables such as gender, age and date of first enrolment. KISE only  has  data  of  the  trainees  that  have  graduated  from  the  institute;  the  children assessed; those rehabilitated at the centre and the disjointed results of various surveys.

The fact that many for instance in care giving as well as for their children with special needs  and  sometimes,  the  parents  themselves  may  contribute  to  dropout  or  low transition rates across the various levels of education. Half of the learners who complete Primary  education  transit  to  secondary  schools.  The  ratio  of  secondary  schools  to Primary is comparatively low.

texts.orig: v. Lack of a policy on institutionalised home-based care:  CBC has defined home-based care and learning as an option. However, there is lack of a policy and guidelines, and preparation and resourcing of parents/guardians on provision of home-based care for children with special needs.

texts.orig: vi. Lack of a policy on safety and protection of children with SNE : Children and older learners with special needs are very vulnerable to all forms of abuse. For instance, one of the issues constraining transition of girls is early pregnancy, emanating from sexual exploitation and abuse. The MoE lacks a policy and guidelines for safeguarding these learners  from  the  various  forms  of  abuse.  The  existing  Education  Sector  Disaster Management Policy (MoE, 2017) does not address the safety of learners with special needs and disabilities.

texts.orig: viii. Lack  of  an  institutional  Framework  to  support  functional  assessment:  The  quality standards for EARCs are yet to be approved and availed for use. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 6.4.2 Issues in access and transition
texts.text: 6.4.2 Issues in access and transition

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. Limited access to integrated schools that may be attributed to the low proportion of Primary compared to Secondary schools: Expanding access to SNE in Kenya is highly dependent  on  integrated  schools.  Nearly  90  per  cent  of  all  learners  and  trainees Countrywide are in either integrated or regular schools, whereas available spaces in Special Secondary schools are only around 5 per cent of the Primary school population. In addition, the learning environments in most of these schools are not accommodative of special needs, and therefore remain largely inaccessible.
texts.text: Limited access to integrated schools that may be attributed to the low proportion of Primary compared to Secondary schools: Expanding access to SNE in Kenya is highly dependent  on  integrated  schools.  Nearly  90  per  cent  of  all  learners  and  trainees Countrywide are in either integrated or regular schools, whereas available spaces in Special Secondary schools are only around 5 per cent of the Primary school population. In addition, the learning environments in most of these schools are not accommodative of special needs, and therefore remain largely inaccessible.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Inadequate conceptualisation of SNE Transitions: The BECF (KICD, 2017) defines transitions in the CBC. However, there is need to re-conceptualise these transitions with a  view  to  creating  a  balance  between  academic-based  and  functionality-based transitions in SNE. For instance, the transition from home to Pre-primary is left out, as well as that of institution to independent living.

For instance, the transition from home to Pre-primary is left out, as well as that of institution to independent living.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iii. ' New' areas in SNE : While there are many SNE schools and learning facilities, most of what is available serves the 'traditional' disability areas namely, Hearing, Visual, Mental  and  Physical.  Such  areas  as  Gifted  and  Talented,  and  Emotional  and Behavioural Disorders are not catered for. Yet, CBC implementation implies heavy investment in the various categories of SNE and disabilities.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iv. Failure to take cognizance of SNE in the Kenya University Colleges Central Placement Services  (KUCCPS)  placement  protocols  and  the  resulting  implication  on  Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) funding: Less than 10 per cent of the students enrolled in  TVET  institutions  are  placed  through  KUCCPS.  This  implies  that  most  of  them cannot access HELB, yet they need it most.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 6.4.3 Issues in the Relevance of SNE
texts.text: 6.4.3 Issues in the Relevance of SNE

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. Implementation of CBC curriculum provisions:  The BECF (KICD, 2017) provides for elaborate  curriculum  alternatives  for  learners  with  special  needs  and  disabilities, including  home-based  care,  specialised  curriculum,  specialised  curriculum  with adaptation, and enriched curriculum. These are, however, not supported with the right capacities, materials and proper financing.
texts.text: Implementation of CBC curriculum provisions:  The BECF (KICD, 2017) provides for elaborate  curriculum  alternatives  for  learners  with  special  needs  and  disabilities, including  home-based  care,  specialised  curriculum,  specialised  curriculum  with adaptation, and enriched curriculum. These are, however, not supported with the right capacities, materials and proper financing.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Rigid teacher training curriculum: The current SNE teacher curriculum is still too rigid, with minimal integration of ICTs. Teachers require training in appropriate pedagogy, for effective teaching and learning of learners with special needs and disabilities.
texts.text: Rigid teacher training curriculum: The current SNE teacher curriculum is still too rigid, with minimal integration of ICTs. Teachers require training in appropriate pedagogy, for effective teaching and learning of learners with special needs and disabilities.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iii. Lack of psychosocial and spiritual support: Learners with special needs and disabilities (and their  parents)  experience  childhood  emotional  challenges  and  trauma.  Yet,  the available  psychosocial  support  is  not  adapted  to  cater  for  them.  For  instance,  most religious institutions are unprepared to offer spiritual support to such learners due to lack of SNE skills and knowledge, and language barrier.
texts.text: Lack of psychosocial and spiritual support: Learners with special needs and disabilities (and their  parents)  experience  childhood  emotional  challenges  and  trauma.  Yet,  the available  psychosocial  support  is  not  adapted  to  cater  for  them.  For  instance,  most religious institutions are unprepared to offer spiritual support to such learners due to lack of SNE skills and knowledge, and language barrier.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iv. Lack of adaptation  of  TVET courses: The TVET courses offered do not meet the training needs and interests of learners with special needs and disability and the four specialised TVETs are far too inadequate to meet the transition needs, and skills gap for  the  youth  with  disabilities  nationally.  The  'reverse  integration'  (KISE,  2020), whereby nearly 80 per cent of trainees in special TVETs are without disability, implies the loss of specialised training and attention.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 6.4.4 Issues in the Quality of SNE
texts.text: 6.4.4 Issues in the Quality of SNE

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. Low  learning  outcomes  and  inadequately  adapted  and  modified  assessments  and examinations: Learning outcomes of students with disabilities are significantly lower than for those without disabilities, across all levels. The examination accommodations are inadequate and do not address some disabilities, nor cater for individual needs of the candidates. Assessment in the CBC has also not been adapted to meet the needs of learners with special needs and disabilities.
texts.text: Low  learning  outcomes  and  inadequately  adapted  and  modified  assessments  and examinations: Learning outcomes of students with disabilities are significantly lower than for those without disabilities, across all levels. The examination accommodations are inadequate and do not address some disabilities, nor cater for individual needs of the candidates. Assessment in the CBC has also not been adapted to meet the needs of learners with special needs and disabilities.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Language  deprivation  of  deaf  children  and  use  of  language:  Most  deaf  children, especially those born to hearing parents, do not develop language until later in life. Lack of hearing screening at birth leads to delayed recognition of  Hearing Impairment in some  cases.  There  is  no  existing  support  for  early  language  development  for  deaf children, and no organized outreach services to support the parents.
texts.text: Language  deprivation  of  deaf  children  and  use  of  language:  Most  deaf  children, especially those born to hearing parents, do not develop language until later in life. Lack of hearing screening at birth leads to delayed recognition of  Hearing Impairment in some  cases.  There  is  no  existing  support  for  early  language  development  for  deaf children, and no organized outreach services to support the parents.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iii. Staffing in SNE: TSC estimates that more than 12,000 SNE teachers are needed to address the gap occasioned by the 100 per cent transition policy and the move towards inclusion. At the same time, nearly 90 per cent of the school heads and teachers have no training in SNE. Some teachers in schools for the deaf are not proficient in sign language, while some of those in schools for the blind lack Braille proficiency.

Some teachers in schools for the deaf are not proficient in sign language, while some of those in schools for the blind lack Braille proficiency.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iv. EARCs lack capacity for functional assessment: The majority of SNE CSOs are trained in the four disability areas namely, Hearing, Visual, Physical and Mental (Malasi & Wanyonyi, 2018). There is deficiency of functional assessment capacities in Autism, Gifted and Talented, Deaf-blind, learning difficulties, speech and language disorders; and Behavioural and Emotional disorders. The EARCs are also inadequately staffed, and lack basic facilities.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: v. Poor infrastructure and inadequate devices to remove barriers: The physical infrastructure in most SNE schools does not meet the recommended standards.
texts.text: Poor infrastructure and inadequate devices to remove barriers: The physical infrastructure in most SNE schools does not meet the recommended standards.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: vi. Insufficient integration of ICT in the teaching and learning for learners and trainees with disabilities and special needs: Learners and trainees with disabilities and special needs  are  disadvantaged  in  accessing  ICT  resources.  Access  to  specialised  learning resources, assistive devices, and learning technologies in the SNE institutions is still very low. In addition, ICT infrastructure in the SNE institutions is not adequate in terms of well-equipped computer labs and resource centres.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: vii. Lack of standards and quality assurance mechanisms: The National Education Quality Assurance  and  Standards  Framework  for  Basic  Education  (MoE,  2021)  does  not provide for adequate regulation and management of the SNE sub-sector. There is need for a quality and standards mechanism and tools, as well as a reporting mechanism that adequately addresses the concerns of SNE.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 7.1 Introduction
texts.text: 7.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  chapter  analyses  conceptualization  and  design  of  the  Competency  Based  Assessment (CBA) for effective curriculum reforms implementation. This is guided by the principles of Competency  based  Curriculum  (CBC)  as  outlined  in  the  Basic  Education  Curriculum Framework (BECF; KICD, 2017). Given the importance of assessment in the learning process, a paradigm shift is required, from over-reliance on summative assessment to a balance between summative  and  formative  assessments  with  emphasis  on  the  formative  aspect  that  allows continuous appraisal on learning progress and feedback. The four parameters that guided the Taskforce in discussions on assessment are: Purpose of the assessment; Mode of assessment; Tools to be used in the assessment; and Reporting procedure of the assessment outcomes.

Given the importance of assessment in the learning process, a paradigm shift is required, from over-reliance on summative assessment to a balance between summative  and  formative  assessments  with  emphasis  on  the  formative  aspect  that  allows continuous appraisal on learning progress and feedback. The four parameters that guided the Taskforce in discussions on assessment are: Purpose of the assessment; Mode of assessment; Tools to be used in the assessment; and Reporting procedure of the assessment outcomes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter is organized in 6 main sections excluding this introduction. First is explanation of key  concepts,  followed  by  a  situational  analysis  of  assessment  at  various  levels  of  Basic Education in Kenya. The next section explores international best practices on CBA followed by  a  section  on  stakeholder  submissions  and  engagements.  The  final  section  presents  the Taskforce recommendations on CBA.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Assessment, rubrics are tools that guide the interpretation and grading of learners' work against a set criteria or standard. Also referred to as 'criteria sheets', 'grading schemes', or 'scoring guides', these outline the criteria and descriptors of expected performance of learners at various levels. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 7.3.1.2   Assessment at Primary Education level
texts.text: 7.3.1.2   Assessment at Primary Education level

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The 8-4-4 system entails various formative (classroom) assessments which teachers administer in form of oral/aural questioning, observations and written tests during the learning process. Individual school policies are used to guide the written tests administered on either weekly, monthly and/or termly basis. The Kenya Certificate of Primary Education (KCPE) examination is a summative norm-referenced examination conducted at the end of the eight-year Primary education course to compare a learner's performance to that of others in the same cohort. Its main purpose is selection and placement of learners into the various public Secondary schools, which are categorized into National, Extra-County, County and Sub-County schools. Private Secondary schools also use the results for admission.

Individual school policies are used to guide the written tests administered on either weekly, monthly and/or termly basis. The Kenya Certificate of Primary Education (KCPE) examination is a summative norm-referenced examination conducted at the end of the eight-year Primary education course to compare a learner's performance to that of others in the same cohort. Its main purpose is selection and placement of learners into the various public Secondary schools, which are categorized into National, Extra-County, County and Sub-County schools. Private Secondary schools also use the results for admission.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In terms of the mode of administration, the KCPE examination is conducted once a year to the entire Standard 8 cohort for a period of three days. It is purely pen and paper except for learners with special needs and disabilities who may use paper and machine (computer, TV or braille machines). The examination has seven (07) subjects which are tested in nine (09) papers as detailed in Annex 7.1. A learner is expected to sit for six (06) subjects in total. The test items are in form of Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) for all the papers except for Kiswahili Insha, English and Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) Compositions which are in essay format.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For purposes of reporting , a candidate's performance is quantified in terms of scores attained out of a possible 100 marks per subject, which are combined and reported out of 500 marks, where 05 is the lowest and 500 marks is the highest score. Reporting is also described using Grades, in which Grade A is described as Very Good, while Grade E is described as Poor (see Appendix 7.1). Since the results are used for placement in Secondary schools, the higher the learner's  score,  the  higher  the  probability  of  being  selected  into  what  is  perceived  as competitive Secondary schools.

Since the results are used for placement in Secondary schools, the higher the learner's  score,  the  higher  the  probability  of  being  selected  into  what  is  perceived  as competitive Secondary schools.

texts.orig: The mode of administration for the KCSE examination is mainly pen and paper except for learners with special needs and disabilities who may use paper and machine (computer, TV or braille machines). texts.label: text
texts.orig: The tools used  to  administer  the  examination include a combination of project, theory and practical  papers.  KNEC  prepares  project  papers  and  related  guidelines  (including  tasks milestones) and scoring guides. These are sent to schools at the beginning of the year to enable teachers assess the subjects and the scores submitted to KNEC. KNEC monitors the milestones to ensure reliability of the assessment and scoring. The six subjects with a project component are: Agriculture, Art and Design, Woodwork, Metalwork, Building Construction and Computer Studies. Twelve subjects; Chemistry, Physics, Biology, Home Science, KSL, Music, Art and Design, Power Mechanics, Electricity, Drawing and Design, Aviation and Computer Studies have a practical paper administered alongside the theory papers at the end of the year.

texts.text: 7.3.1.4   National Assessments to Monitor Learner Achievement

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The MoE through KNEC conducts periodic sample-based National Assessments at various levels  of  Basic  Education  to  monitor  learning  achievements  as  well  as  other  intervening variables  including  the  learning  environment,  learner  and  teacher  characteristics  that  could affect learning. The purpose of the assessments which are administered at Standard 3, 6, 7 and Form 2 is  to  assess  the  quality  of  education  and  monitor  learning  achievement. Tools are developed  to  assess  literacy,  numeracy,  sciences  and  Life  Skills  as  well  as  the  learning environment. The mode of assessment is sample-based assessment; administered and scored by KNEC. Reporting is  done  through a National report which gives feedback on levels of learning  achievements  and  the  effect  of  various  inputs  to  acquisition  of  the  desired competencies.  The  Government  and  education  stakeholders  use  the  results  of  the  national assessments to design targeted interventions to improve the quality of learning.

texts.orig: 7.3.2 Issues relating to Assessments in the 8-4-4 System
texts.text: 7.3.2 Issues relating to Assessments in the 8-4-4 System

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Six pertinent issues relating to assessments conducted in the 8-4-4 system, some of which had also been cited by previous Education Commission and Taskforce reports were identified as follows: (i) inadequate guidelines for assessment at Pre-primary level; (ii) over-emphasis on summative assessment on a limited selection of learning areas that bestow 'academic success' on a relatively small proportion of the learners; (iii) the high-stakes nature of assessments that overrides the essence of learning; (iv) broad coverage of curriculum at Secondary Education level with limited specialization; (v) unintended use of examination results that create failures; and (vi) inadequate inclusion in the assessment of learners with special needs including those with disabilities, the Gifted and Talented.

texts.orig: 7.3.2.3 Broad  coverage  of  curriculum  at  secondary  education  with  limited  room  for specialization
texts.text: 7.3.2.3 Broad  coverage  of  curriculum  at  secondary  education  with  limited  room  for specialization

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the 8-4-4 system at Secondary school level, learners are allowed to select subjects at Form 3. The criteria for selection does not adequately provide room for specialization. This is due to the fact that out of the seven minimum subjects which a learner is graded against; (i) three subjects (English, Kiswahili and Mathematics) are compulsory; (ii) at least two are selected from the Science cluster (of Biology, Chemistry and/or Physics); and, (iii) at least one subject from the Humanities (History & Government / Geography / Religious Studies). Therefore, the learner  is  only  left  with  a  choice  of  one  subject  from  the  technical,  industrial  and  foreign languages.

For most learners, the KCSE examination has not been sufficient in identifying their competencies for appropriate placement at Tertiary level.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: International policies such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UNESCO, 2019) and  Sustainable  Development  Goal  (SDG)  No.  4  advocate  for  inclusive,  equitable  quality education and promotion of lifelong learning opportunities for all. Section 18(2) of the Persons with Disabilities Act , (2003), emphasizes that learning institutions shall take into account the needs  of  learners  with  disabilities  with  respect  to  the  entry  requirements,  pass  marks, curriculum, examinations, auxiliary services, use of school facilities, class schedules, physical education requirements among others.

texts.orig: Although various forms of affirmative action have been put in place for learners with special needs  and  disabilities  in  the  8-4-4  system,  focus  has  been  mainly  on  learners  with  visual, hearing, physical and mild mental impairments. texts.label: text
texts.orig: A  Gifted  and  Talented  individual  is  one  with  outstanding  talents  and  giftedness,  and capabilities of remarkable performance when compared with others of their age, experience and environment in one or several areas. Details on this category of learners are provided in Chapter Six on Special Needs Education (SNE).  Key policy and regulations developed for learners with special needs in the 8-4-4 education do not address the education needs of Gifted and Talented learners. These include the (i) 8-4-4 syllabus; (ii) Sector Policy for Learners and Trainees with Special Needs and Disabilities (MoE, 2018); and (iii) KNEC Regulations on Examinations and Assessment.

texts.orig: In  the  education  reforms,  the  CBA  focuses  on  informing  learners,  teachers,  parents  and guardians on continuous learning progress. It is based on a mode of assessment that entails continuous and formative techniques relevant to the educational level of the learner; and, is mainly administered by the class teachers in a classroom setting during learning and using assessment tools that are appropriate for each level. texts.orig: 7.4.1 International Best Practices on CBA
texts.text: 7.4.1 International Best Practices on CBA

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Literature from international best practices emphasises a shift from the traditional testing of acquisition of knowledge and skills, towards assessment that focuses on individual learners' acquisition  of  competences  through  application  of  knowledge . The  current  global  trends advocate for the use of more performance-based assessment methods which integrate real life contexts and learning activities. Assessments should also be geared towards giving feedback on learners' progress, rather than creating a ' pass or fail ' dichotomy (Care & Vista, 2017).

The  current  global  trends advocate for the use of more performance-based assessment methods which integrate real life contexts and learning activities. Assessments should also be geared towards giving feedback on learners' progress, rather than creating a ' pass or fail ' dichotomy (Care & Vista, 2017).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Accordingly, Hammond et al. (2013) recommended designing of CBA in the United States' education system, with emphasis on assessments that (i) assess higher-order cognitive skills; (ii) are applicable in the real world; (iii) apply internationally benchmarked best practices; (iv) support instruction and learning; (v) are valid, reliable, and fair. In terms of relevance to the 21 st Century,  educational  assessment  must  be  geared  towards  moulding  productive  and engaged  citizens  equipped  with  cognitive,  social  and  technological  skills  which  enable evaluation and application of knowledge to the contemporary societal needs. According to Care and Kim (2020), CBA provides room for the assessment of critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, information literacy and communication.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In  Europe,  there  has  been  a  shift  in  assessment  from traditional testing  to  assessment  of competencies since the 1990s (Semire, 2003). In addition to one-off summative examinations, other alternative tools and formats of assessment have been widely adopted in order to provide learners with opportunities to develop and demonstrate 21 st Century skills, values and attitudes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In England, the statutory National Curriculum assessments are conducted in Years 2 and 6 and at General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) examination level, taken in Year 11. At the  end  of  Key  Stages  1  and  2,  the  process  includes  a  combination  of  tests  and  teacher assessment judgements. The key elements to the statutory assessment process in Key Stage 1 are Standard Attainment Tests (SATs) and teacher assessment. The SATs are used to support the teacher's judgement.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The teacher assessments which are recorded as the statutory assessment outcomes are reported in Reading, Writing, Mathematics and Science. For each subject, teachers use the available evidence  to  reach  one  of  a  number  of  judgements,  guided  by  the  national  assessment framework.  The Teacher Assessment describes learners' performance in three broad abilities: ' Above Expected Standard', 'Expected Standard' and 'Below Expected Standard' .  Learners with  special  needs  in  education  are  assessed  using  a  separate  grading  system.  The  criteria applied at Key Stage 2 vary across the subjects because of the different skills targeted.

During the third and fourth year of Secondary school (S3 and S4), learners take seven or eight subjects including Mathematics and English. texts.orig: A learner wishing to study a subject at a higher level is required to attain a credit level (Grade 1  or  2).  As  with  GCSE,  most  Standard  Grade  subjects  have  a  coursework  element,  which accounts for the final mark. To guide selection and placement into Independent Public Schools, Senior  Schools  offer  pre-tests  for  learners  from  age  11  to  build  up  a  short-list  of  suitable applicants. The tests are Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) administered online, annually; disseminated to all schools the examinees had applied; for use in selection and placement. The Common Entrance Examination for learners of age 11+ consists of English, Mathematics and Science, taken over two days with extension questions provided for learners who are relatively more able. Entrance Examination for learners of age 13+ is set by the Independent Schools Examinations  Board  (ISEB)  although  some  Independent  Schools  set  and  mark  their  own examinations.

texts.orig: In Finland , the key role of assessment is to improve instruction and learning (Finnish National Board  of  Education,  2010).  Assessment  is  performance-based,  mainly  formative  and continuous, infused in classroom activities. Assessment rubrics are provided in the National curriculum  to give  common  assessment  criteria  across  all  schools.  Teachers  provide meaningful individualized support to learners. Formative classroom assessment is aligned to the  national  criteria.  The  final  assessment  undertaken  at  the  end  of  Basic  Education  is conducted  by  subject  teachers  and  includes  samples  of  learners'  performance  for  two subsequent years. Reporting of assessment outcomes is qualitative, using descriptions ranging on a scale, from ' very good ' to ' needs practice '. Numerical grading is not used.

texts.text: 7.4.1.2 Assessment Practices in USA and Canada

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In USA , curriculum development, implementation and assessment is organized at state, school, district and national associations' levels, hence there is no centralized education system. The education  system  consists  of  Primary  (5  years);  Junior  Secondary  (3  years);  and  Senior Secondary (3  years). Assessment is undertaken continuously throughout the year to ensure learners are on track, using multiple-layered assessment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the British Columbia province of Canada , the curriculum has been re-designed to be more flexible and individualized, with assessment aimed at demonstrating learners' competency in higher order skills. Learners are permitted to choose how they 'show what they know' and hence:  demonstrate  competency  on  deeper  learning  outcomes.  This  maximizes  innovation, personalization, creative thinking and collaboration. It enables identification of learning needs, assessment of competency, evaluation of learning progress and provision of timely, meaningful feedback on learning. It also addresses the needs of diverse learners in different contexts. The curriculum sets standards for guiding classroom instruction and assessment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Shanghai, China , one of the distinct features of the curriculum reforms introduced in 1998 was 'Alternative Assessment' .  This was necessitated by the deficiencies noted in traditional assessment (Moss, Girard, & Haniford, 2006), and the high stakes nature of examinations that were used for ranking and placement of learners. Chinese examination formats were revised from  being  mainly  multiple  choice  questions  and  close-ended  questions  to  open-ended, analytical, innovative and inquiry-oriented assessment tasks (Jiang, 2017, 4).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An attempt was made to infuse development of the desired non-cognitive aspects of traditional Chinese culture, ideologies, moral character, spirit and practical ability, physical and mental health, and interests and talents in assessment (Shanghai Municipal Education Commission, 2014). Further, the 'Green Academic Evaluation System' was introduced, aimed at a shift in assessment,  from  being  academic/examination-oriented,  to  include  assessment  of  learners' moral conduct, physical and mental well-being (Tan, 2017; Dong, 2013).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  first  high  stakes  assessment  in  Japanese  schools  is  the  entrance  examination  to  upper Secondary school, which determines admission. Each category of upper Secondary school has its  own admission processes and requirements. Admission is extremely competitive, and in addition to entrance examinations, the learner's academic work, behaviour, attitude, and record of participation in the community are also taken into account. Teachers at all levels of schooling consistently assess their learners through teacher-developed tests and other forms of learners' work. Japan also administers national assessments - the National Assessment of Academic Ability (NAAA) - in Grades 6 and 9.

texts.text: 7.4.1.4 Assessment Practices in Africa

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In South Africa , school-based continuous assessments are incorporated during awarding and grading  of  learners  in  the  Secondary  school  exit  qualification,  constituting  25%  of  the assessment at final Grade 12 (Tikly et al ., 2018). Some of the challenges raised with regard to school-based assessments were: subjectivity of continuous assessment marks as evidenced by the  weak  correlation  between  continuous  assessment  and  summative  examination  scores (Shepherd & Van der Berg, 2015); poor uptake by teachers; lack of monitoring and support; learner discipline; and parental involvement (Ramalepe, 2015).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Egypt ,  school-based  assessments  (which  are  mainly  teacher-made)  are  conducted  at  all levels. Regional examinations are conducted at Grade 6 under the supervision of the National Centre for Examinations and Evaluation. At the end of lower Secondary (Grade 9), learners take a national examination with those passing being awarded a Basic Education Completion Certificate. Placement in Senior Secondary depends on learners' performance and acquisition of Basic Education Completion Certificate. Secondary education has 3 tracks: (i) general which takes  three  years,  (ii)  vocational/technical  which  takes  3-5  years,  and  (iii)  dual  system vocational  known  as  Mubarak-Kohl  schools  which  runs  parallel  to  the  others.  Those  in vocational schools are awarded a Certificate in Vocational Education. Monthly tests are also administered by teachers for the first two years and a national examination is taken at Grade 12for award of a Certificate of GSE.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ghana, the education system comprises Primary (6 years), Junior Secondary (3 years), Senior  Secondary  (3  years)  and  University  (4  years).  A  Basic  Education  Certificate Examination (BECE) is offered at the end of Junior Secondary (Form 3) in seven subjects. Admission to Senior Secondary is competitive as learners are placed in the different categories of schools: National schools (Public and Private); Public Boarding Schools and International Private Schools offering IB or A level. The school-based assessment is weighted at 30% while the final examination constitutes 70% in the final Senior Secondary certificate. In school-based assessment,  assignments  constitute  40%,  continuous  assessments  constitute  40%  while  the projects constitute 20%. The total 100% is then scaled down to 30% and is then combined with the 70% of the final examination.

texts.orig: 7.4.2 Global perspectives in addressing special needs of gifted and talented learners
texts.text: 7.4.2 Global perspectives in addressing special needs of gifted and talented learners

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Over the years, education for the Gifted and Talented learners has not been well defined in Kenya and yet studies reveal that if the Gifted and Talented learners are not well identified and harnessed, society will have lost. Further, it has been established that Gifted learners can also be found among students who do not perform well in academic examinations (Davis et al. , 2011; Goodhew, 2009) resulting in these learners being consequently classified inadvertently as under-achievers. Kenya may gain some useful insights from countries that have a history of recognizing and responding to the educational needs of Gifted and Talented learners.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In USA, education  for  Gifted  learners  is  not  regulated  at  the  federal  level,  although recommendations by the US Department of Education are offered. However, since each Gifted learner  has  unique  attributes,  individualized  information  on  the  learner's  performance  and potential  is  collected  through  a  combination  of  objective  (quantifiably  measured)  and subjective  (personally  observed)  identification  instruments.  Districts  follow  a  systematic, multi-phased process for identifying gifted students to find those who need services beyond the general education programme. These phases are: (i) nomination or identification phase; (ii) screening or selection phase; and (iii) placement phase.

Sample rating scales include Scales for Rating Behavioural Characteristics of Superior Students, Purdue Academic Rating Scale, portfolios and performances (Renzulli & Smith, 1977). Portfolios or work that is collected over time should include student reflections of their products and/or performances for both academic (Language, Arts, Mathematics) and creative (Speech, Arts, Music) pursuits. An academic or artistic  case  study  approach  may  be  used  and  may  include  data,  observations,  and  growth demonstrated in various settings.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Canada , the Peel District School Board has various high schools with Regional Enhanced Programmes to provide students an opportunity to develop and explore skills in a particular area of interest. Under the 'Regional Enhanced Program', learners identified as Gifted may choose to attend such schools instead of the mainstream schools. In the Regional Enhanced Program,  Gifted  learners  take  core  courses  (English,  Mathematics,  and  the  Sciences)  in  a responsive  environment  alongside  fellow  Gifted  peers.  Their  assignments  are  modified  to encourage individual creativity.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Hong Kong the Education Commission Report No. 4 issued in 1990 recommended a policy on  Gifted  education  for  schools  in  Hong  Kong  and  suggested  that  a  broad  definition  of giftedness using multiple criteria should be adopted. A three-tier Gifted education framework was adopted in 2000. Levels 1 and 2 are recognized as being school-based while Level 3 is the responsibility of the Hong Kong Academy for Gifted Education (HKAGE). Level 1 serves the entire school population irrespective of ability; Level 2 deals with between 2-10 percent of the ability group; while Level 3 caters for the top 2 percent of learners to facilitate development of specialized programmes in specific learning areas outside the regular classroom that allows systematic teaching for learners with outstanding performance in specific domains.

texts.label: text

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The purpose of assessment at the Lower Primary level is two-pronged. Firstly, it will help to establish the level of mastery of core competencies, knowledge and skills in the learning areas and  secondly,  it  will  inform  learners,  parents  and  policy  decision  makers  on  the  learning progress  and  areas  needing  intervention.  At  this  level,  the  mode of  assessment  will  be formative, undertaken by teachers during learning within or outside the classroom between Grades 1 and 3. A national School Based Assessment (SBA) will be conducted at the end of Grade 3. KNEC will develop the assessment tools, while teachers will administer, score and give feedback to the learners.

Learners with special needs and disabilities following the Stage-Based Curriculum will also be assessed in learning areas covered under the Foundation level.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Learners with special needs and disabilities following the Age-based (regular) Pathway shall be assessed using tools developed for their peers in the Age-based (regular) Pathway, with appropriate  modifications,  adaptions  and  other  forms  of  accommodations  on  the  tools  and mode of assessment, depending on each learner's individual needs.  For learners following the Stage-based Pathway, assessment will seek to identify and nurture individual interests, abilities and potential with a view to enhancing independent, self-fulfilling and self-sustaining life with minimal or no support. Due to their varied limitations, the mode of assessments will be mainly formative, administered by teachers using the appropriate approaches and tools .

texts.text: 7.6.4 Assessment of the Gifted and Talented (G&T) Learners

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For the first time in Kenya, learners who are Gifted and Talented have found a space in the context of SNE. These are learners whose potential is distinctly above average in one or more of four domains: intellectual, creative, social and physical (IBE, 2013; Glossary of Curriculum Terminology). Oftentimes, such giftedness or talents are either ignored or undiscovered for lack of awareness that may result in labelling the learners as disruptive, non-focused children who eventually lack the teachers or parental attention in the learning process (Kang'ethe &
texts.text: For the first time in Kenya, learners who are Gifted and Talented have found a space in the context of SNE. These are learners whose potential is distinctly above average in one or more of four domains: intellectual, creative, social and physical (IBE, 2013; Glossary of Curriculum Terminology). Oftentimes, such giftedness or talents are either ignored or undiscovered for lack of awareness that may result in labelling the learners as disruptive, non-focused children who eventually lack the teachers or parental attention in the learning process (Kang'ethe &

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Mokua, 2020).  Assessment  of  Gifted  and  Talented  learners  will  serve  the purposes of  (i) identifying  the  giftedness  and  talents  in  the  learner  to  guide  on  appropriate  placement;  (ii) inform on mastery of competencies and readiness for transition; and, (iii) provide feedback to learners, parents, teachers in subsequent grades as well as curriculum developers and other stakeholders involved in curriculum implementation on required interventions for the learners.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For Gifted and Talented learners, the mode of assessment will entail a systematic, multi-phased process which will start with identification of learners who exhibit exceptional giftedness or talent by  their teachers. The  teachers  will have  been  provided  with  guidelines  that accommodate a wide range of giftedness, to be interpreted variably, since each gifted learner has  unique  attributes.  Schools  will  then  refer  such  learners  to  the  regional  Educational Assessment Resource Centres (EARCs) and/or the Assessment and Research Centre (ARC) at KISE for comprehensive diagnostic assessment / screening.

Schools  will  then  refer  such  learners  to  the  regional  Educational Assessment Resource Centres (EARCs) and/or the Assessment and Research Centre (ARC) at KISE for comprehensive diagnostic assessment / screening.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The assessment, which will require collaboration with teachers and parents/guardians, will be formative, continuous, assessing both behavioural and academic characteristics to advice on the required interventions and placement, as detailed in Chapter 6. Upon placement, the mode of assessment of the learners will be determined by individual placement, and upon successful completion of the relevant course work as shall be recommended by the school and EARCs. The time for administration shall be flexible and learner-guided, whenever the learner is ready, providing adequate time for task completion depending on the pace of the learner.
