texts.orig: The two key accommodations which will be necessary for the Gifted and Talented learners are: (i) Curriculum enrichment which will entail provision of additional and advanced subject / learning  area  content,  methodology,  resources,  time  and  assessment;  and  (ii) Acceleration which will involve multiple grade progressions or grade skipping within a school year, while providing for the social development of the learner. Acceleration may or may not necessarily involve the physical movement of the learner to another class or institution.  Depending on the circumstances, the individual learner's developmental and learning needs will be addressed without physical re-location. Regulations shall be developed to guide and ensure appropriate identification, enrichment and acceleration of Gifted and Talented learners.

texts.orig: 8.1. Introduction
texts.text: 8.1. Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  chapter  presents  the  conceptualization  and  design  of  Competency  Based  Teacher Education (CBTE) at Pre-service level. It is organized in four major sections excluding this introduction. Definitions of key concepts in Teacher Education (TE) are presented followed by a  detailed  situational  analysis  of  the  current  status  of  Pre-service  Teacher Education (PTE) which includes a brief history of TE, a review of the previous Education Commission and Taskforce Reports; overview of PTE at various levels, and teacher management. Further, a section on insights from international benchmarking, needs assessment on curriculum reforms for  TE  and  stakeholder  submissions  are  presented  respectively.  The  chapter  ends  with recommendations on various aspects of PTE in the context of CBTE.

Further, a section on insights from international benchmarking, needs assessment on curriculum reforms for  TE  and  stakeholder  submissions  are  presented  respectively.  The  chapter  ends  with recommendations on various aspects of PTE in the context of CBTE.

texts.text: 8.2.1 Philosophy of Education and Teacher Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Philosophy of education is the branch of applied or practical philosophy concerned with the nature and broad aims of education and the issues arising from its theory and practice. Over the centuries, the concept of education has attracted Western philosophical thinking from both the  general  and  technical  perspectives.  In  relatively  recent  times,  African  philosophers  of education have also made their contributions as noted by Njoroge and Bennaars (1986) in their book Philosophy of Education in Africa. According to Njoroge and Bennaars, education is characterized as having four dimensions that jointly make its operationalization a truly human phenomenon. These are the cognitive, normative, creative and dialogical dimensions .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are four dimensions to be mainstreamed in the conceptualization and design of TE. These dimensions may be interpreted as the acquisition of knowledge and skills (i.e. understanding the 'what and how'); values (engagement with norms of worthwhileness); problem solving (critical, analytical and innovative abilities) and social interaction skills (engaging in dialogue with  others).  The  Koech  Report  (GoK,  1999)  postulates  that  a  'national  philosophy  of education should be driven by the need to fashion individual growth and development into a sound and effective citizen' (GoK, 1999:6). The report argues for an 'Afrocentric philosophy of  education  that  guides  the  content  and  methods  of  the  Kenyan  curriculum,  design  and practice' (RoK, 1999:7).

In doing this, theory tends to be concerned with general rather than specific issues about phenomena. This suggests, inevitably, that theory can be considered as partial (Widdowson, 2003). texts.label: text
texts.orig: Generally, in TE, the main approaches that have been identified in literature as being dominant at one point or the other, in different contexts, since the 1960s are: Process-Product approach, Practical  (School  [institution]  Based)  approach,  Task  Based  approach,  Reflective  Teacher Education, and Competency Based TE (Korthagen, 2001; Kumaravadivelu, 2006; Richards & Rodgers, 2014). Approaches, in turn, give emphases to various methods; which in this context are  defined  as  the  actual  class  or  lecture  room  pedagogical  interactions  and  activities  that teacher educators and student teachers are engaged in as they cover the prescribed content (Darling-Hammond, 2006; Richards & Rodgers, 2014; Larsen-Freeman, 2010). Some of the most  dominant  methods  in  TE  include  lectures,  collaborative  teaching  and  learning, inquiry/reflective tasks, demonstrations, dramatization and coaching/observation methods.

CBTE focuses on teacher ability to perform specific relevant, appropriate and strategic tasks within a participatory problem-solving and collaborative pedagogical context that appreciates individual learner effort and achievement (Richards & Rodgers, 2014).

texts.orig: 8.3.1 Brief History of Teacher Education in Kenya
texts.text: 8.3.1 Brief History of Teacher Education in Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Formal TE was introduced in Kenya by the European missionaries in the early 19 th Century and was organized to reflect the European TE systems. The missionaries 'trained' the student teachers at the intermediate schools to be able to meet the demands for teachers in the mission and the so-called 'bush' schools that the missionaries had created (Bashiruddin, 2018). The trainees were of relatively low qualifications though they were considered to be among the well-educated of the time (Kafu, 2003). At the time, teacher education was not well organized.
texts.text: Formal TE was introduced in Kenya by the European missionaries in the early 19 th Century and was organized to reflect the European TE systems. The missionaries 'trained' the student teachers at the intermediate schools to be able to meet the demands for teachers in the mission and the so-called 'bush' schools that the missionaries had created (Bashiruddin, 2018). The trainees were of relatively low qualifications though they were considered to be among the well-educated of the time (Kafu, 2003). At the time, teacher education was not well organized.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: According to Anderson (1965), the Beecher Commission Report, which was produced before Kenya's independence (1943), had created some order in Primary and Secondary Education although it had ignored TE. In the 1950s initial formal Teacher Training Colleges (TTCs) were constructed with the first ones being Siriba and Kagumo in 1956. During this time, there were concerted efforts to coordinate and standardize TE in Kenya. This led to establishment of the Kenya Institute of Education (KIE) in 1964 (Nyankanga et al ., 2013). After independence, on the recommendations of the Kenya Education Commission Report (also Ominde Commission, 1964)  the  Government  of  Kenya  (GoK)  consolidated  the  Primary  TTCs  to  18  with  each admitting 600 students to address the massive shortages especially of African teachers.

texts.orig: 8.3.2.1 Pre-Primary Teacher Education
texts.text: 8.3.2.1 Pre-Primary Teacher Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  TE  Course  for  Pre-primary  teachers,  known  as  Early  Childhood  Development  and Education (ECDE) course is offered at Certificate, Diploma and Degree levels in various public and private TTCs in Kenya. The Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) develops the ECDE TE curriculum. Most of the practising ECDE teachers underwent a two-year course consisting of six residential sessions during the school holidays at the then District Centres for Early Childhood Education (DICECE) under coordination of the National Centre for Early Childhood Education (NACECE). Currently, most ECDE teachers are trained in the regular TTCs. According to NESSP (MoE, 2018), there was notable growth in the number of ECDE attributed to the availability of the trainings as noted below:
texts.text: The  TE  Course  for  Pre-primary  teachers,  known  as  Early  Childhood  Development  and Education (ECDE) course is offered at Certificate, Diploma and Degree levels in various public and private TTCs in Kenya. The Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) develops the ECDE TE curriculum. Most of the practising ECDE teachers underwent a two-year course consisting of six residential sessions during the school holidays at the then District Centres for Early Childhood Education (DICECE) under coordination of the National Centre for Early Childhood Education (NACECE). Currently, most ECDE teachers are trained in the regular TTCs. According to NESSP (MoE, 2018), there was notable growth in the number of ECDE attributed to the availability of the trainings as noted below:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Trained ECDE teachers grew by 34.5 per cent, from 83,814 in 2013 to 112,703 in 2018. It is probable that the employment of more teachers by the County Governments may have motivated untrained ECD teachers to go for training, as manifested in the reduction of  the  number  of  untrained  ECD  teachers  by  39.4  per  cent  over  the  same  period. Furthermore, the number of ECD teacher training colleges grew from 131 in 2013 to 280  in  2018,  with  private  training  colleges  accounting  for  most  of  the  ECD  teacher training opportunities . (MoE, 2018:56-57)

texts.orig: The Taskforce Survey (2020) established that public TTCs in Kenya had an enrolment of 8,551 trainees, of whom 3,217 were male while 5,334 were female. 939 tutors were engaged to teach the  second  year  trainees  in  these  colleges,  implying  an  increase  in  the  number  of  trained teachers.  Unlike  in  the  Pre-primary  TTCs,  there  was  comparatively  balanced  gender representation in the enrolment of the male and female trainees. This is critical in ensuring availability of both male and female teachers to act as role models as well as to handle gender specific issues relating to the female and male learners.

However, records for a number of the private PTE TTCs were not captured. This indicates a need by the Ministry of Education (MoE) to ensure registration of all private TTCs with a view to regulating the quality of training. Primary  and  Early  Childhood  Education  Option  or  distinct programmes for Primary Teacher Education or Early Childhood TE. They also admit students directly through the Kenya Universities and Colleges Placement Service (KUCCPS).

texts.orig: The  Diploma  in  Secondary  Teacher  Education  (DSTE)  was  offered  in  three  public  TTCs; namely: Kagumo, Kibabii and Lugari and 23 private TTCs. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Humanities. In recent years, the DSTE does not attract many trainees as potential applicants opt  for  University  Education.  According  to  NESSP  (2018-2022),  the  number  of  Diploma teacher trainees declined by 5.6 per cent from 2,158 in 2018 to 2,037 in 2019. The decline in enrolments for the DSTE course may be attributed to the fact that the minimum entry Grade of C+  in  the  KCSE  examination  is  also  the  Grade  required  to  qualify  for  admission  into University. With far less students attaining the C+ Grade since 2016, the Universities absorb all the KCSE candidates who attain the mean grade of C+ and above.

texts.orig: 8.3.2.5 University Based Secondary Teacher Education
texts.text: 8.3.2.5 University Based Secondary Teacher Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Universities offer a Bachelor of Arts (BA) with Education or Bachelor of Science (B.Sc.) with Education. The B.Ed. Degree is a four-year programme offered by a total of thirty-two (32) accredited Universities to secondary school graduates with a minimum KCSE mean Grade of C+  and  C+  in  two  subjects  offered  at  Secondary  school  level.  According  to  KUCCPS  a candidate requires at least a C (plain) in English to undertake any teaching degree programme. This is in addition to the minimum cluster points set by respective Universities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Applicants are also required to score a minimum of D+ (plus) in Mathematics to qualify for admission into a B.Ed. (Arts) course. Those seeking admission for the Science courses require a minimum of C (plain) in Mathematics and C+ (plus) in any of the Science subjects offered in the Secondary school curriculum. The B.Ed. course has two major components: the teaching subjects  (content)  and  the  professional  components.  The  professional  component  includes: Educational  Psychology,  Educational  Foundations,  Educational  Leadership/management, Curriculum Studies and General/Subject Instructional Methods. TP is compulsory and trainers must pass to qualify for award of the B.Ed. certificate (Otunga et al. , 2011).

texts.orig: 8.3.2.6 Post-Graduate Diploma in Education (PGDE)
texts.text: 8.3.2.6 Post-Graduate Diploma in Education (PGDE)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are sixteen (16) Universities that offer Postgraduate Diploma in Education (PGDE) to candidates with undergraduate qualifications in subjects undertaken in the Secondary school curriculum,  but  lack  professional  training  in  education  to  qualify  as  teachers.  The  average length of the PGDE is one academic year. The Taskforce noted that both the B.Ed. and the PGDE options are acceptable in the Kenyan context as long as the minimum number of hours for  professional  courses,  teacher  support  courses,  content  courses,  micro  teaching  and Practicum are attained.

texts.orig: 8.3.2.7 Special Needs Teacher Education (SNTE):
texts.text: 8.3.2.7 Special Needs Teacher Education (SNTE):

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Special  Needs  TE  (SNTE)  is  offered  by  KISE  at  both  Certificate  and  Diploma  levels  to professionally qualified practising teachers who are holders of the PTE certificate [also, P1 teachers]). The KISE Diploma is a two-year programme while the Certificate course lasts one year. KISE also manages a National Psycho-educational Assessment Centre, a Pre-Primary school to model inclusive education, and produces teaching and learning materials and assistive devices for SNE among other functions (MoE, 2018). Figure 8.2 shows the KISE Diploma in SNE  graduates  by  gender  between  2015  and  2019.  This  will  form  the  basis  for  making projections and planning for the SNE teachers required in the sector. The data indicates that fewer men train in this area compared to women.

texts.orig: To qualify for award of the PTE Certificate, a trainee must pass TP assessment and obtain a pass in all the eight subjects offered. The final Grade - Distinction, Credit, Pass, or Fail - is determined by scores in the six best performed subjects. As demonstrated in Table 8.2, the pass rate in the PTE examinations in public TTCs declined from 90% in 2014 to 45% in 2019. The trend is replicated in private TTCs during the same period, with the pass rate dropping from 81% in 2014 to 43% in 2017 and 65% in 2019. This raises concerns over quality of the training and the classroom teaching by the trainees.

texts.text: 8.3.3 Teacher Educators

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Teacher  educators  or  tutors  educate  and  support  student  teachers  to  develop  professional, content and pedagogical knowledge, values and competencies for teaching and facilitation of other  curricula  requirements.  They  act  as  role  models  for  student  teachers  (Lunenberg, Korthagen, & Swennen, 2007). A review of literature, and insights from international best practices reveals that many Countries have developed programmes designed to prepare their Teacher Educators for colleges and Universities. However, in many instances, the development of expertise and an identity as a teacher educator is a process most teacher educators go through alone (Lunenberg & Hamilton, 2008).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TSC is mandated to manage teachers in Kenya as articulated in Article 237 of the Constitution of Kenya (2010) and the TSC Act (2012). The  requirements  specified  for  registration  of  applicants  bear  implications  on admission of students into TE institutions and the conceptualization and design of PTE in the context of CBC as outlined herein:

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.3.4.3 Continuous Teacher Professional Development (CTPD)
texts.text: 8.3.4.3 Continuous Teacher Professional Development (CTPD)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While teachers acquire the foundations of content and pedagogical knowledge through their college and University pre-service programmes, they are expected to continue learning through CPD to ensure quality support for students' learning and achievement in tandem with changing educational  needs.  Trilling  and  Fadel  (2009:124)  suggest  that  'teachers  must  become  21 st Century learners themselves, learning from inquiry, design, and collaborative approaches that build a strong community of professional educators'.
texts.text: While teachers acquire the foundations of content and pedagogical knowledge through their college and University pre-service programmes, they are expected to continue learning through CPD to ensure quality support for students' learning and achievement in tandem with changing educational  needs.  Trilling  and  Fadel  (2009:124)  suggest  that  'teachers  must  become  21 st Century learners themselves, learning from inquiry, design, and collaborative approaches that build a strong community of professional educators'.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Section 11(e) of the TSC Act, (2012) mandates the Commission to facilitate career progression and professional development for teachers. Other Semi- Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) responsible for CTPD include the KICD, KNEC, Centre for Mathematics, Science and Technology Education in Africa (CEMASTEA) and the Kenya Education Management Institute (KEMI). Although the Taskforce ToR on TE was specific to pre-service training, it became  apparent  that  CTPD  is  necessary  for  the  teachers  and  other  critical  stakeholders involved in implementation of the CBC. This calls for induction and reorienting the teachers already in service; qualified teachers outside employment- before or upon employment; school heads  and  managers  of  educational  institutions.  Overall,  the  Taskforce  noted  the  need  for coordinated CTPD by an institution modelled around the Kenya School of Government.

texts.orig: 8.4.1.1 Enhancing rigor in the selection process of teacher trainees
texts.text: 8.4.1.1 Enhancing rigor in the selection process of teacher trainees

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The top-performing world education systems recruit their teachers from the top best performing third of each cohort graduating from their school system as noted in the top 5 per cent in South Korea, the top 10 per cent in Finland, and the top 30 per cent in Singapore and Hong Kong (Barber & Mourshed, 2007, p. 16). Japan requires that teachers successfully complete rigorous induction programmes before permanent appointment to the teaching position (Wang et al. , 2009; in Ingvarson et al. , 2013 p. 154).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.4.1.2 Employing effective quality assurance policies and procedures
texts.text: 8.4.1.2 Employing effective quality assurance policies and procedures

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Strong Quality-Assurance (QA) processes characterize effective TE programmes which may be within education faculties, across whole Universities or both. In Japan, each teacher-training institution conducts a self-evaluation prior to the accreditation process that is scheduled every seven  years.  The  Japan  Institution  conducts  external  accreditations  for  Higher  Education Evaluation (Tatto et al. , 2013). Under the TE Act of 2002 and the Teacher Enforcement Rules of  1995,  Chinese  Taipei  has  clear  quality  control  mechanisms  at  every  stage  of  TE,  from selection through to certification.

texts.orig: 8.4.1.3 Limiting the number of places in teacher training to match demand
texts.text: 8.4.1.3 Limiting the number of places in teacher training to match demand

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In Singapore, Finland and Chinese Taipei, the number of places in teacher training is limited by  projections  of  demand  for  new  teacher  recruits  and  workforce  requirements  (Barber  & Mourshed, 2007). This makes demand the driver of TE and training.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 8.4.1.4 Working in partnerships with schools to train teachers
texts.text: 8.4.1.4 Working in partnerships with schools to train teachers

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Most  high-performing  TE  school  systems  work  in  partnerships  with  specially  designated schools to train teachers as noted in Finland, where all eight TE institutions work in partnership with 'training schools'. The teacher-training schools exist for all levels of schooling and may include the Pre-primary level (Tatto et al. , 2013). This is the case as well in Chinese Taipei, Singapore, and Germany among other high-performing education systems. This partnership has  contributed  to  improvement  of  the  quality  of  University  and  school  teaching  staff, cooperation in mentoring, supervising and assessing pre-service teachers in designated schools.

texts.text: 8.4.1.5 Investing in high mastery of content and research skills

In Finland, for instance, every student must complete a master's thesis that presents original research in either education or the subject(s) they intend to teach.

texts.orig: Further, to be qualified as a subject teacher in a Finish comprehensive school (Years 7-9), a teacher must have completed a Master's Degree that includes 35 study weeks in a subject that is taught in comprehensive schools in addition to 35 weeks of pedagogical studies. texts.orig: 8.4.1.6 Exploring Africa Agenda 2063 on Teacher Education
texts.text: 8.4.1.6 Exploring Africa Agenda 2063 on Teacher Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Objective 1 of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA) aims to: 'Revitalize the teaching profession to ensure quality and relevance at all levels' and this has a bearing on achievement of the African Union (AU) Agenda 2063. The Strategy foregrounds the status of TE in Africa as critical to achievement of the Agenda 2063 vision of integration, peace and prosperity, by facilitating acquisition of skills, knowledge; requisite values and attitudes; hence the need to assure the status of TE (CESA 16-25).

texts.text: The  Taskforce  reviewed  the  KICD  TE  Needs  Assessment  study  of  2017  to  establish  the necessary reforms in PTE. The objectives covered issues of structure of TE, competencies expected of teachers, resources needed, pedagogical approaches and assessment appropriate for the various PTE courses. The study also explored reforms desired in CTPD. This study yielded several recommendations for reformation of TE, including:

Degree  with  opportunities  for professionalism,  comprehensive  content  knowledge,  appropriate  pedagogical  skills  and integration of values as well as Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs) and other relevant 21st Century skills. texts.orig: Considering some of the new learning areas in the CBC, especially in some of the SSS Tracks, some stakeholders expressed a need for a PGDE to equip graduates of general content areas with pedagogical skills to cater for specialized learning areas. This would be in addition to enabling those with Diploma in general content areas to undergo courses that would earn them a Diploma in Secondary TE (DSTE). Stakeholders observed that the intellectual demands of the  CBC require applicants for PTE  - at Pre-primary  and Primary  school levels  - to have attained at least a Mean Grade of C (plain) in the KCSE examination. This would also enable them cope with the rigour of the Diploma in TE.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Regarding designs of the PTE programmes, three main issues emerged from the stakeholder engagements.  The  first  was  the  need  to  have  TE  in  Pre-primary,  Primary  and  Secondary Education respectively. Hence, the students admitted into PTE programmes would have similar entry grades and pursue standardized professional courses, except for deviations related to the target  learners.  Stakeholders  were  further  categorical  that  SNE  TE  trainees  be  required  to initially take a TE course in Pre-primary, Primary or Secondary education before admission into a higher Diploma in DSNE. Some stakeholders advocated for pre-service admission of students  into  the  DSNE  programmes,  citing  the  relative  success  of  this  approach  in  some Universities. However, most stakeholders supported the post-service route.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter presents a conceptualization of the design and implementation of programmes for Parental Empowerment and Engagement (PEE), Value-based Education (VbE) and Community Service Learning (CSL). The chapter is organised in five sections excluding this introduction and contextualisation. The ensuing sections address the major areas of focus in the  chapter  and  describe  the  broad  related  concepts,  situational  analysis  and  views  from stakeholders. Finally, the Taskforce recommendations for PEE, VbE and CSL are presented thematically.

texts.orig: The Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECF; KICD, 2017) acknowledges that the lives of learners beyond the classroom and school include their families and communities. Learners traverse these social spaces interacting with social and environmental agents that are critical in supporting learning through what is popularly known as Communities of Practice.

Learners traverse these social spaces interacting with social and environmental agents that are critical in supporting learning through what is popularly known as Communities of Practice.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Communities of Practice refer to groups of people who share a joint concern in the activities of a specific domain in which they hold a stake and hence, learn how to engage better together as they continually interact regularly (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder, 2002). texts.orig: 9.2.1 The Whole Child Approach (WCA) and the Whole School Approach

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  WCA  is  conceptualised  within  the  context  of  Bronfenbrenner's  Systems  Ecological Theory and perceives a child's environment as a nested series of interconnected systems. These foster all areas of children's development and learning, from social to emotional and cognitive skills to literacy, spiritual, numeracy, and other competencies. Within the CBC reforms, the WCA offers  a  relatively  strong,  supportive  approach  to  children  as  they  transit  from  prePrimary to Senior Secondary School (SSS).
texts.text: The  WCA  is  conceptualised  within  the  context  of  Bronfenbrenner's  Systems  Ecological Theory and perceives a child's environment as a nested series of interconnected systems. These foster all areas of children's development and learning, from social to emotional and cognitive skills to literacy, spiritual, numeracy, and other competencies. Within the CBC reforms, the WCA offers  a  relatively  strong,  supportive  approach  to  children  as  they  transit  from  prePrimary to Senior Secondary School (SSS).

texts.text: Learners' development and acquisition of values is influenced by three dimensions (PEE, VbE and CSL) which transcend schooling into lifelong education. The WCA utilizes a mixture of learning  experiences  across  PEE,  VbE  and  CSL  within  the  following  five  (5)  learning environments as described in Bronfenbrenner's Systems Ecological Theory:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: a) Most-immediate  environment which  is  also  known  as  the micro-system is  the smallest and nearest setting in which the child lives. It includes the home, school or day-care facility, class-teacher, peer group and nearest community of the child. Here, positive parenting plays a crucial role in learning of values, thus making VbE provided at home by parents and teachers at school very critical.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: b) Intermediate environment, also known as the meso-system, is the intermediate setting of the child. This creates relations between home and school; between peer group and family,  and  between  family  and  community.  This  includes  the  child's  immediate family, peers, residence, place of worship and school. Children find themselves here, in their daily routines while parents, teachers, and the immediate community play a significant  role  in  value  acquisition  or  learning.  This  enhances  VbE  as  a  critical foundation upon which CSL begins to emerge, as beneficial learning experiences.

texts.text: 9.3 Parental Empowerment and Engagement (PEE) Concepts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: PEE is one of the guiding principles of the BECF (KICD, 2017). Parental empowerment is undertaken to enhance the capacity of parents or guardians to enable them actively participate in  the  holistic  development  of  their  children  in  and  out  of  school.  Empowerment  refers  to enhancement of knowledge, skills, values, attitudes and practices of an individual or a group in pursuit of a mutual goal. PEE is important because parents are a child's first teacher in all matters of life. It is the process of becoming better prepared and more confident in performing one's role as a parent/guardian as cited by Xaba (2015, p. 205):

texts.orig: Connor and Cavendish (2018) indicate that the main focus of empowerment is to ensure that parents take an active role in decision making in matters pertaining to the life of their children. Parental engagement is therefore the active participation of parents or guardians and critical caregivers in their children's learning, spiritual, emotional, social and mental development. Parents  can  aid  children  in  lifelong  learning  by  creating  a  conducive  atmosphere  at  home whereby the learners can experience more of what they learnt at school. At the same time, parents can work in collaboration with teachers to support character formation and learning for their  children.  The  parents/guardians  are  allowed  the  opportunity  to  actively  support  the learning experiences of their children at home, in school and in the community.

texts.orig: An ethnographic  study  conducted  in  South  Africa  among  historically  disadvantaged  black Secondary school learners interrogated the effects of black parental involvement on the success of their children. Over a period of two years (2002/03), the study focused on 24 parents of learners  in  eight  different  Historically  Disadvantaged  Secondary  Schools  (HDSS).  The findings  revealed  that  the  parents'  role  was  crucial  in  the  enhancement  of  learner  success. Parents  who  played  little  or  no  role  in  their  children's  homework  and  study  programmes emerged as  having  contributed  to  the  poor  performance  of  their  children  in  the  classroom (Singh, Mbokodi & Msila, 2004: 301).

texts.orig: Another  study  by  Abuya et  al .  (2014)  focusing  on  1,200  girls  in  Kibra  (Kenya)  applied education  intervention  packages,  with  one  intervention  involving  parental  participation. Evidence  from  this  study  revealed  that  girls  who  enjoyed  parental  involvement  in  their schooling demonstrated significant improvement in their educational aspirations by increasing their mean scores compared to those not exposed to the parental involvement. These studies suggest  strongly  that  parental  participation  in  their  children's  schooling  has  significant potential not only in shaping and moulding children's educational outcome but also character.

texts.text: 9.3.1.1 Insights from Best Practices

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Best practices on PEE from Scotland, Germany and Australia advocate for models that view parents  as  partners  in  learning,  social,  mental  and  emotional  development  of  the  children (Schnell, Crul, Fibbi, & Montero-Sieburth, 2015). In these Countries, schools have tailored interventions to parent and child needs, parent/family voices, peer support, development of culturally  relevant  programmes,  inclusion  of  fathers  and  school  governance.  This  calls  for development of a Framework to strengthen family-school partnerships amongst school leaders, teachers and school teams.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Available literature shows that PEE is practised in many Countries in Europe, Australia and Africa (KICD, 2018). In Scotland, for instance, parents are seen as partners in the learning process,  with  parental  involvement  legislation  having  been  put  in  place  to  impact  on educational, economic and social outcomes. In Germany, parents are entitled to involvement in administrative and academic decisions. They are able to make decisions on transition of learners from Grade 4 to 5.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In addition, they participate in conferences and advise on career pathways. Comparatively, in Australia, Family-School Partnerships Framework has been established to address partnerships amongst school leaders, teachers and school teams. Similarly, the National Parents' bodies give voice in the formulation of education policy. Furthermore, the South African Schools Act of 1996 has empowered parents and communities by granting them formal power to participate in education. However, most parents in South Africa are not involved due to challenges posed by illiteracy and lack of relevant knowledge.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since 1963, parents in Kenya have played a role in schooling, through support of development programmes and participation in Parents Teachers Association. The Kenya Constitution, 2010 provides for the right to parental care and protection, notwithstanding the importance of values (Section 53 (e) and 56 (d)). The Kamunge Report (GoK, 1988) articulated the role of parents as 'financing of education and training' (p.15). The Odhiambo Report (MoE, 2012, p. 206) recommended  development  of  'guidelines  for  a  mentoring  programme  for  parents  and guardians  at  different  stages  of  children's  development  in  order  to  empower  them  with appropriate  parenting  skills'.  The  report  also  recommended  involvement  of  parents  and guardians in the mentoring of the young people'.

texts.orig: Travis Hirsch's (1969)  Social  Bonding  Theory argues  that  persons  who  have  strong  and abiding attachments to conventional society based on the form of attachments, involvement, investment, and belief are less likely to deviate from norms compared with persons who have weak or shallow bonds. Arguably, a child's intellectual ability is influenced by their genetic makeup and nurtured by socio-environmental conditions. Hence, behaviour can be modified through organization of the environment. Since the earliest bonds formed by children are with their  caregivers  (majorly  parents),  parental  engagement,  if  well  harnessed,  has  potential  to continue impacting the child throughout their life.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Values are basic and fundamental beliefs and principles that guide or motivate attitudes or actions and help people to determine what is important to them. Values describe the personal qualities that individuals embody, guide their actions; the person they want to be; the manner in which they treat themselves and others, and their interaction with the world. Accordingly, values provide the general guidelines for conduct (Steven, 2018).

Accordingly, values provide the general guidelines for conduct (Steven, 2018).

texts.orig: In addition, the Sessional Paper No. 8 of 2013 on National Values and Principles of Governance holds that a nation's values define a people's identity. Thus, values are fundamental beliefs of a  nation  that  guide  the  choices,  actions  and  behaviour of its  citizens.  National  values  exert influence on the way citizens and communities engage. Since values are behaviour-based, the drivers include families, communities, educational institutions; leaders in religious and faithbased organizations (Sessional Paper No. 8 of 2013). In essence, values determine a person's character and collectively, character defines a nation, thus underscoring the critical reason for their anchoring in the BECF (KICD, 2017) as a core pillar.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The BECF (KICD, 2017) has advanced that VbE should be mainstreamed in all learning areas using the formal, informal and non-formal dimensions of education. Values are addressed in the learning outcomes, learning resources, pedagogy and learning experiences, instructional supervision, Pre-service Teacher Education (PTE), teacher professional development, teacher management and school policies. The mainstreaming of values will be based on the WSA and WCA models.  The  formal,  non-formal  and  informal  curriculum  dimensions  constitute  the logical entry points for mainstreaming VbE in schools.
texts.text: The BECF (KICD, 2017) has advanced that VbE should be mainstreamed in all learning areas using the formal, informal and non-formal dimensions of education. Values are addressed in the learning outcomes, learning resources, pedagogy and learning experiences, instructional supervision, Pre-service Teacher Education (PTE), teacher professional development, teacher management and school policies. The mainstreaming of values will be based on the WSA and WCA models.  The  formal,  non-formal  and  informal  curriculum  dimensions  constitute  the logical entry points for mainstreaming VbE in schools.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The formal learning dimension is the institutionalized, intentional and planned learning (IBE, 2013:27). In the formal dimension, most subjects or learning areas are well suited to host VbE. The  non-formal  learning  is  institutionalized,  intentional,  planned  and  covers  programmes contributing to youth and children literacy, as well as programmes on life skills, work skills, and  social,  spiritual  and  cultural  development  (IBE,  2013:45).  Informal  learning  includes learning activities that occur in the family, workplace, through the media, local community and daily life, on a self-directed, family-directed or socially-directed basis (IBE, 2013:31). These may be intentional or deliberate but not necessarily institutionalized.

texts.orig: The WSA and WCA adopt a holistic approach in promoting learners' health and well-being (ASCD, 2020). This is predicated on the assumption that VbE is a systemic programme or intervention that must be directed at the entire school context rather than just at individual learners.  Patterson et  al. (2020) explains that schools can increase engagement with their communities to enhance VbE, thus securing sustainable improvement in the learners' overall successes. In the WSA, all aspects of the school community have potential to impact positively upon each learner's value system.

texts.orig: Oral  and  written  submissions  from  key  stakeholders  including  FBOs,  PAs,  Educationists, Professional Associations, Universities, Government institutions among others were analysed and, the following observations made. Stakeholders observed a dearth in capacity to mentor, coach and adopt appropriate pedagogy in inculcating values both at school and community levels. They expressed the need for Continuous Professional Development (CPD) and adequate resourcing by all stakeholders for efficient and effective implementation of VbE (Task Force, 2019; Report on Rapid Response Survey of the Viewpoints of CBC Master Trainers). This was in addition to expressions indicating that all teachers should be helped to understand the role of values in human life to ensure that they are in harmony with what they are expected to teach, regardless of whether they are teaching CBC or 8-4-4 (FGD-11M/BUS).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The WSA is designed to stimulate the nurturing of values and ethics directly, through infusing these in the formal curriculum, and the indirect method, through the non-formal, informal and the hidden curriculum. The direct method emphasizes the mainstreaming of the eight (8) core values in the whole curriculum and whole teaching-learning process. The curriculum designs, schemes of work and lesson plans should indicate the methods of nurturing the core values in each learning area, and the content taught (EMACK, 2011). Similarly, indirect (non-formal) methods should include school assembly, co-curricular activities, team games, study clubs, and social service programme, and the celebration of religious activities, among others.
texts.text: The WSA is designed to stimulate the nurturing of values and ethics directly, through infusing these in the formal curriculum, and the indirect method, through the non-formal, informal and the hidden curriculum. The direct method emphasizes the mainstreaming of the eight (8) core values in the whole curriculum and whole teaching-learning process. The curriculum designs, schemes of work and lesson plans should indicate the methods of nurturing the core values in each learning area, and the content taught (EMACK, 2011). Similarly, indirect (non-formal) methods should include school assembly, co-curricular activities, team games, study clubs, and social service programme, and the celebration of religious activities, among others.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Similarly, the informal curriculum should constitute the mode of conveying values, through talking trees and walls, which engrave critical messages in the form of fliers and adverts on walls and trees. This would help nourish the values of cooperation and mutual esteem, honesty and integrity, discipline  and social obligation.  Further, the school authorities need to make deliberate efforts to holistically plan, spring up and utilize experiential activities to promote values amongst learners. Thus, an integrated approach is employed where all the learning areas have a component of value orientation (Luther, 2001) and also using different curricular modes of the formal, non-formal and informal hidden curriculum (Indrani, 2012).

texts.orig: 9.5 Community Service Learning (CSL)
texts.text: 9.5 Community Service Learning (CSL)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: CSL is an educational activity or programme that entails experiential learning whereby learners engage in formally approved learning with a focus on real life contexts outside the school setting  that  link  schools  with  their  communities,  thus  enhancing  civic  responsibility,  and strengthening citizenship ( Delve, Mintz, & Stewart, 1990).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The BECF (KICD, 2017) proposes CSL as a trans-disciplinary skill to be experienced from early  years of learning to the end of Junior Secondary School (JSS). At the SSS, CSL is a mandatory stand-alone subject required for graduation at Grade 12. The BECF (KICD, 2017) also proposes that CSL is made mandatory in all Tertiary institutions as well as a requirement for graduation and entry to employment.

texts.orig: Thus, volunteer programmes lie at the extreme left end of the continuum, while internship programmes lie in the extreme right end and CSL is in-between them. Sigmon (1994) further explains that, as with volunteer programmes, CSL implies self-sacrifice and charity. However, the same CSL, as described by Furco (1996), involves more structure and student obligation than do volunteer programmes. Honnet and Poulsen (1989) further present CSL as entailing the inherent selflessness as is requisite in volunteer programmes whereby participants render themselves as service-focused, designed to benefit the service recipient.

texts.orig: A review of literature on Rwanda, Uganda, Ghana, South Africa, Israel, South Korea, Russia, USA, United  Kingdom,  Australia  and  Germany  revealed  that  CSL  was  practised  in  many Countries  in  North  and  South  America,  United  Kingdom,  Asia  and  also  in  Africa  (KICD, 2018).  This  focused  majorly  on  social,  environmental,  cultural  and  political  engagement. Community service is used in these Countries to foster nationalism and citizenship, mutual responsibility, sacrifice and selflessness, service, among others.

texts.orig: The  UNICEF  report  on  Every  Child  Learns  Strategy  (2019-2030)  advocates  for  a  strong support for community engagement in education for improvement of learning outcomes. A team of researchers carried out a study on community service and service learning in public schools in the United States (Keilsmeie et al. , 2004). This was aimed at determining the impact of community service and service learning on learner achievement. The study was nationally representative  and  targeted  principals  and  other  administrators  in  Grade  12  (K-12)  public schools in the United States.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The study revealed that 69 per cent of Grade 12 public schools engage learners in community service, totalling an estimated 15 million learners and 8 out of ten principals in schools that offer service learning stated that it had a positive impact on academic achievement and the community viewed the youth as a resource.

texts.orig: According to the Community Service Order Act of 1998, community service was a punishment for offenders who had been convicted or sentenced by a court for an offence under the written law.  This  led  to  a  negative  attitude  among  Kenyans  on  community  service  yet  overtime, community service has enabled learners to contribute towards improvement of their community as a learning opportunity. The Gachathi Report (GoK, 1977) recommended 'bringing about a sense of dignity towards  social service and productive labour  through appropriately programmed activities of basic education' (p. 12).

It was further proposed that CSL activities be organized in such a manner that they impact the community in which schools are situated.  Emphasis was on design of affordable, age-appropriate, relevant and sustainable services as is exemplified in the following excerpts:

texts.text: 9.5.2.4 Theories of CSL

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Theories have shown that learning happens best through experience in the social context. Giles et  al .  (1994)  examine  Dewey's  experimentalism  with  an  emphasis  on  the  principles  of experience, inquiry, and reflection as the key elements of a theory of understanding servicelearning. They posit that the principles of interaction and continuity in Dewey's philosophy on experiences form an experiential continuum. In this regard, the role of the teacher in shaping and  directing  experiences  that  fit  into  this  continuum  becomes  critical.  This  thinking  is corroborated by Schumer's (1993b) assertion that learning results from the transaction between the individual (learner) and the environment.

They posit that the principles of interaction and continuity in Dewey's philosophy on experiences form an experiential continuum. In this regard, the role of the teacher in shaping and  directing  experiences  that  fit  into  this  continuum  becomes  critical.  This  thinking  is corroborated by Schumer's (1993b) assertion that learning results from the transaction between the individual (learner) and the environment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Vygotsky (1997) proposes that environmental experiences be provided to enable learners test and  revise  their  models.  This  will  enable  connections  between  the  previous  and  current perceptions  of  learners  while  allowing  them  the  freedom  to  construct  their  own  meaning. According to Cherry, K. (2019, concrete experience provides information that serves as a basis for  reflection.  From  these  reflections,  learners  assimilate  the  information  form  abstract concepts and use these concepts to develop new learning experiences about the world, which they then actively test. This then actualizes the CSL experience.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 10.1 Introduction
texts.text: 10.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter discusses the policy and legal issues necessary for effective curriculum reforms implementation. The situational analysis entails a review of the various relevant policies and legislations that govern the education sector, identifying existing gaps, conflicts and overlaps, which  require  revisions  that  will  support  effective  implementation  of  the  CBC. Thus,  this chapter builds onto the key legal Frameworks and policies informed by the recommendations of the Odhiambo Report (2012) Taskforce on Re-Alignment of the Education Sector to the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which were actualized by Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019.
texts.text: This chapter discusses the policy and legal issues necessary for effective curriculum reforms implementation. Thus,  this chapter builds onto the key legal Frameworks and policies informed by the recommendations of the Odhiambo Report (2012) Taskforce on Re-Alignment of the Education Sector to the Constitution of Kenya (2010) which were actualized by Sessional Paper No. 1 of 2019.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter is presented in four main sections excluding this introduction. The sections entail firstly, a situational analysis that highlights international education protocols to which Kenya is a signatory; National policy as well as recommendations from stakeholder submissions and engagements.  Second is analysis and identification of gaps in policy and legal provisions that require action. Finally, the chapter presents recommendations on the gaps in policy and legal frameworks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Constitution of Kenya (2010) explicitly recognizes the right to education in Articles 10, 11,  43,  53,  54,  56,  62,  63,  66,  174,  175,  176,  189,  201,  226,  227  and  248.  Among  other provisions, these address the need for free and compulsory Basic Education and affordable Tertiary Education, training and skills development; affirmative action in favour of minorities and marginalized groups; values, transparency and accountability in education governance.

Among  other provisions, these address the need for free and compulsory Basic Education and affordable Tertiary Education, training and skills development; affirmative action in favour of minorities and marginalized groups; values, transparency and accountability in education governance.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: The Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya
texts.text: The Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In  actualizing  the  provisions  to  education,  Articles  185(2),  186(1)  and  187(2)  of  the Constitution  have  mandated  the  National  Government  to  develop  education  policies  and curriculum; maintain standards; and manage examinations and university charters. The County Government is assigned responsibility to oversee Pre-primary Education, village polytechnics, home  craft  centres,  and  childcare  facilities.  This  implies  the  need  for  a  close  working relationship between the National and County Government for effective provision of education.

texts.orig: 11.1 Introduction
texts.text: 11.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  chapter  focuses  on  Monitoring  and  Evaluating  (M&E)  of  the  curriculum  reforms implementation.  Firstly,  the  chapter  presents  explanation  of  key  concepts  followed  by  a situational analysis of the status of M&E of the education system in Kenya. This is based on a review  of  related  literature,  stakeholder  engagement  and  submissions.  Thirdly  the  chapter presents recommendations on strategies to establish an effective M&E  system  for implementation of the curriculum reforms.

texts.text: 11.2 Key Concepts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Monitoring entails an ongoing, systematic generation of evidence that informs assessment of progress towards achievement of set objectives, outcomes, outputs and impacts of a selected intervention (UNESCO, 2013). In the case of curriculum reforms implementation, monitoring will entail gathering information on the objectives of Competency based Curriculum (CBC) to ensure the intended procedures are followed and the curricula are aligned to set objectives.
texts.text: Monitoring entails an ongoing, systematic generation of evidence that informs assessment of progress towards achievement of set objectives, outcomes, outputs and impacts of a selected intervention (UNESCO, 2013). In the case of curriculum reforms implementation, monitoring will entail gathering information on the objectives of Competency based Curriculum (CBC) to ensure the intended procedures are followed and the curricula are aligned to set objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Evaluation is a systematic and objective assessment of ongoing or completed interventions to ascertain their impacts and/or outcomes. Curriculum evaluation entails measuring and judging the extent to which the courses, programmes, learning activities and opportunities expressed in the  curriculum  Frameworks actually  produce  the  expected  results  (UNESCO,  International Bureau of Education, 2013). Evaluation of the curriculum reforms implementation will seek to examine  the  results  chain  (including  the  inputs,  activities,  processes,  envisaged  outputs, outcomes and impacts), to establish the extent of attainment of the objectives.

This will entail consolidation of information on the progress in schooling as the basis for any necessary interventions, while also facilitating planning.

texts.orig: Well-functioning  M&E  systems  have  mechanisms  to  support  and  balance  vertical  and horizontal, internal and external accountability. External mechanisms include national school evaluations and/or large-scale learner assessments while internal mechanisms include school self-evaluation,  staff  appraisal  and  school/classroom-based  learner  assessments.  Consistent with  the  2019  Global  Education  Monitoring  (GEM)  Report,  a  comprehensive  CBC  M&E system will facilitate assessment of the Country's progress towards attainment of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 and its targets, as well as other related education targets in the SDG agenda such as equity and quality in education and training.

texts.orig: Global practices show that most Countries have created frameworks that integrate internal and external Quality Assurance (QA) mechanisms in the M&E system. These include inspectorates, national  learner  assessments,  school  self-evaluation  and  teacher  appraisals.  Evidence  from Finland,  China  and  Australia  demonstrates  the  value  of  systematic  review  of  educational programmes  and  processes  to  maintain  and  improve  their  quality,  equity  and  efficiency (McLoughlin  and  Visser,  2003).  These  also  emphasize  the  need  for  mechanisms  (tools, processes  and  actors)  and  cognizance  of  the  varied  country-specific  contexts  within  the common aim of supporting teaching and learning.

texts.orig: The Basic Education Act (2013) mandates County Education Boards (CEBs) to coordinate and monitor  education  and  training  at  their  respective  levels  of  jurisdiction,  on  behalf  of  the National and County Governments. The CEBs are expected to collaborate with institutional Boards of Management (BoMs), principals and heads in the management of Basic Education institutions. Among other functions, the CEBs collaborate with the relevant national bodies to register and maintain data banks of education and training institutions under their jurisdiction. CEBs also collaborate with the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) and private schools on teacher  management.  They  prepare  and  submit  comprehensive  school  termly  and  annual reports including Educational Management Information System data to the Cabinet Secretary (CS) in charge of Education on all areas under their mandate.

texts.label: list_item

Lack of a comprehensive system for M&E for curriculum reforms implementation and the need to strengthen monitoring capacity in curriculum relevance and quality vis-avis the labour market demands. texts.label: list_item

texts.label: list_item

Adopt a multi-dimensional M&E approach for curriculum reforms implementation that would  entail  quality  checks  on  input  (human,  material,  and  financial),  process (teaching-learning and management), outputs, learning outcomes and quality of results. This  will entail  (a)  compliance  monitoring  focusing  on  inputs,  (b)  diagnostic monitoring  focusing  on  the  reforms  implementation  processes,  (c)  performance monitoring focusing on outputs, and (d) impact evaluation focusing on outcomes and relevance of the CBC to the labour market.

texts.orig: 12.1 Introduction
texts.text: 12.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  chapter  discusses  Standards  and  Quality  Assurance  (SQA)  for  effective  curriculum reforms implementation in Basic Education and Training. It begins with a brief section on explanation  of  the  key  concepts  in  SQA  in  education,  followed  by  a  situational  analysis capturing the mandate and scope of the SQA, operational reporting structures, human resource, infrastructure  and  funding,  and  challenges  that  are  linked  to  the  various  levels  of  Basic Education.  An  exploratory  review  of  related  literature,  plus  insights  from  stakeholder submissions and engagement as well as from best global best practices informs the next section on recommendations that will facilitate continuous improvement of the quality of education in basic education and training.

texts.text: 12.2 Key Concepts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Quality Assurance (QA) encapsulates the ideas of ' standards ' and ' excellence '.  Standards connote a level of expected excellence or quality of  a  process, outcome or product. In this context, the concept of ' quality ' implies the degree/standard of excellence measured against other things of a similar kind not only locally but internationally. Quality is ascertained through a declaration of confidence that is supported by verifiable evidence. The National Educational Sector  Strategic  Plan  (NESSP  2018-2022)  defines  QA  as  the  process  of  setting  standards, monitoring, and enforcing compliance with the standards.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Schedule 4 of the Constitution (2010) on the sharing of functions between the National and County  Government  assigns  the  development  of  education  policies,  curriculum,  QA  and standards; management of examinations and University charters to the National Government.
texts.text: Schedule 4 of the Constitution (2010) on the sharing of functions between the National and County  Government  assigns  the  development  of  education  policies,  curriculum,  QA  and standards; management of examinations and University charters to the National Government.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The QAS mandate is exercised by the Directorate of Quality Assurance and Standards (DQAS) with responsibilities that encompass development, maintenance and improvement of SQA in Basic Education and Training. The Directorate conducts SQA assessment for supervision of curriculum  implementation  and  provides  continuous  coaching  and  mentorship  support  to practising teachers. It monitors education quality and standards and participates in curriculum development and evaluation at the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) and Kenya  National  Examinations  Council  (KNEC)  respectively.  It  also  prescribes  education quality standards, formulates and implements policies on SQA. The DQAS also conducts talent identification  and  development  in  basic  education.  It  implements  vetting  for  licensing  of expatriate teachers, conducts certification of professional documents; and, conducts capacity building of stakeholders who include teachers, administrators and as well as other relevant.

texts.orig: Further, the Directorate of Schools Audit (DSA) at the Ministry of Education (MoE) conduct financial audit and capacity development of institutional Boards of Management (BoMs) on risk management. The DSA reports are intended to reinforce the DQAS' standards assessment reports and therefore envisioned to inform policy decisions, prudent utilization of resources and thus contributing to enhancement of the quality of learning outcomes. Section 11C the of the Teachers' Service Commission (TSC) Act of 2012 mandates the TSC to undertake QA activities as well as review the standards of teacher training and fitness to teach for persons entering the teachers service, as well as manage the supply of teachers nationally. The role of TSC  in  maintaining  standards,  alongside  other  QA  bodies  and  County  Education  Boards (CEBs) is further acknowledged in Part IX Section (67) of the Basic Education Act (2013).

texts.orig: From  the  foregoing,  it  is  clear  that  in  the  process  of  supporting  quality  education,  the conceptualization of SQA is based more on a structure than on a system. Hence, the Directorate, which is characterised by a largely hierarchical structure, coupled with the staffing status, poses a challenge to accountability and reporting on SQA of the curriculum reforms implementation. The decentralized structure of education governance compartmentalizes the DQAS and TSC functions  into  specialization  areas  that  have  a  clear  chain  of  command;  is  guided  by standardized  protocols  that  govern  decision  making;  and  is  also  designed  to  hold  staff accountable  based  on  department-specific  performance  targets.  Education  stakeholders expressed concern over the lack of a comprehensive SQA system that could be used by both the DQAS at the MoE and the TSC.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Directorate's establishment was 350 SQA officers, compared with the DPSM approved establishment  of  1,056.  These  are  recruited  by  the  MoE  through  the  Public  Service Commission, directly from the teaching force and deployed to the National, Regional, County and Sub-County education offices to oversee the SQA mandate. The SQA officers report to the PS; Director, QAS; Regional Directors of Education (RDEs), County Directors of Education (CDEs) and Sub-County Directors of Education (S-CDEs) respectively (see Appendix 12.2).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Some  officers  are  seconded  to  the  MoE  Directorates  and  Semi-Autonomous  Government Agencies (SAGAs) to support SQA related functions and the ratio of SQA officers to Basic Education and Training institutions ranged from 1:200 to 1:280 on average. As a result of the staff shortage, the Counties were staffed with a CQASO at a minimum; and 67 Sub-Counties had lacked an SQA officer since 2012. The positions of Primary and Secondary CQASO and Sc-QASO were not operationalized. In addition, subject officers were not designated at the Sub-County  level  and  several  Sc-QASOs  were  required  to  pool  together,  to  facilitate  the standards assessments.

texts.orig: The routine and advisory assessment is based on five dimensions: Institutional leadership and management; Curriculum organization and management; Learners' welfare; Physical facilities; and Community involvement. The major operational guidelines for SQA of Basic Education and Training are the Quality Index (MoE, 2010) and the Guidelines for Registration of Basic Education  Institutions  (revised,  2017).  This  broadly  categorizes  the  SQA  indicators  into context, input, process and output indicators.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Context  indicators  address  learners'  characteristics;  socio-cultural  and  economic  aspects; staffing levels; qualifications and competence. Input indicators primarily measure deployment and use of financial, material and human resources (including teaching staff, textbooks etc.). Process  indicators  measure  whether  educational  programmes  are  conducted  to  the  desired standard of quality (including teaching and learning quality, time on task, school climate and leadership).  Output  indicators  reveal  how  the  education  system  is  performing  in  terms  of subject knowledge, competencies, as well as repetition, progression and completion rates.

texts.text: 12.3.5 Emerging issues on SQA from stakeholder submissions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Stakeholder submissions on SQA recommended strengthening of the QA system to harmonize the role of the DQAS and TSC. They also observed the lack of clear education quality standards and indicators that address the CBC, teacher competency, pedagogy, infrastructural safety and instructional resources. The inadequate recruitment of SQA officers was identified as the cause for  inability  by  the  DQAS  to  operate  optimally.  Further,  the  regular  engagement  of  SQA officers  in  administrative  duties  tended  to  draw  them  away  from  their  core  mandate.  The technical capacity and competence of some SQA officers was singled out, compounded by the policing mentality. Stakeholders noted that the Secondary education orientation of most SQA officers had created the tendency to focus more on Secondary compared to Primary and Preprimary education levels.

texts.orig: The unclear backward cascade reporting system from the decentralized education levels to the MoE head office and inadequate attention to the CBC by the CSOs were noted as well, as impeding effective  delivery  of  SQA  services.  Failure  to  empower  school  administrators  to maintain some control over institutional-level SQA practices as well as to share the feedback of  SQA assessments with assessed institutions,  and  inadequate  reporting  and  follow-up  on implementation  effectiveness  were  also  identified  as  impediments  to  education  quality. Stakeholders' submissions on the function of SQA in Basic Education indicated a perceived challenge of quality optimization, process improvement and higher productivity as the DQAS worked to keep pace with the CBC.

texts.orig: 12.4.1 European Union Perspectives on standards and QA
texts.text: 12.4.1 European Union Perspectives on standards and QA

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  European  Union  (2020)  has  demonstrated  that  successful  SQA  frameworks  combine internal and external QA mechanisms. These entail: inspectorates, peer assessment, National student assessments, school self-evaluation, teacher appraisals, and professional networks. The QA mechanisms  also  encompass  a  range  of  tools,  processes  and  actors  to  monitor  policy implementation,  overall  system  performance,  school  and  staff  effectiveness  and  learning outcomes. The European Commission (2020) further suggests eight principles to guide SQA policies, to especially ensure a productive synergy of external and internal QA mechanisms. These are further illustrated as follows:
texts.text: The  European  Union  (2020)  has  demonstrated  that  successful  SQA  frameworks  combine internal and external QA mechanisms. These entail: inspectorates, peer assessment, National student assessments, school self-evaluation, teacher appraisals, and professional networks. The QA mechanisms  also  encompass  a  range  of  tools,  processes  and  actors  to  monitor  policy implementation,  overall  system  performance,  school  and  staff  effectiveness  and  learning outcomes. The European Commission (2020) further suggests eight principles to guide SQA policies, to especially ensure a productive synergy of external and internal QA mechanisms. These are further illustrated as follows:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. Coherence: QA Systems should strive over time to achieve balance and coherence across the different mechanisms developed to meet the demands and expectations of stakeholders within schools and in the wider education system. For instance, Croatia and Slovenia tend to report greater synergy when external QA (macro-level) and IQA (micro-level) data complement and support education quality, and when institutions and stakeholders collaborate to define education improvement strategies .
texts.text: Coherence: QA Systems should strive over time to achieve balance and coherence across the different mechanisms developed to meet the demands and expectations of stakeholders within schools and in the wider education system. For instance, Croatia and Slovenia tend to report greater synergy when external QA (macro-level) and IQA (micro-level) data complement and support education quality, and when institutions and stakeholders collaborate to define education improvement strategies .

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Professional  Learning  Communities: SQA  policies  should  support  professional learning  communities  to  make  best  use  of  SQA  data  for  school  and  system development. In France and Latvia, integrating professional learning and development of human resources into SQA has enabled more students to benefit variously from the support of multidisciplinary teams, cross-sector networks and resource-sharing.
texts.text: Professional  Learning  Communities: SQA  policies  should  support  professional learning  communities  to  make  best  use  of  SQA  data  for  school  and  system development. In France and Latvia, integrating professional learning and development of human resources into SQA has enabled more students to benefit variously from the support of multidisciplinary teams, cross-sector networks and resource-sharing.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iii. Trust and shared accountability: The experiences of Hungary and Norway show that distributing governance responsibility across National, local and school levels realizes a more equal sharing of accountability for learner outcomes, engagement in and support for school development; shared accountability over development of education quality; and reduction in the transaction costs across board. Similarly, trust among SQA actors has been shown to increase cooperation, develop social capital, support innovation and exchange  of  ideas, and  to limit the likelihood of unexpected  interactions or opportunistic behaviour.

Similarly, trust among SQA actors has been shown to increase cooperation, develop social capital, support innovation and exchange  of  ideas, and  to limit the likelihood of unexpected  interactions or opportunistic behaviour.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: iv. Support for innovation: The experience of Slovakia shows that school leaders and teachers need opportunities to take considered risks in order to innovate and develop. On-going M&E of the impact of innovative practice and careful attention to innovation data allows for timely adjustments to new pedagogical approaches while ensuring that students are not left to falter.

On-going M&E of the impact of innovative practice and careful attention to innovation data allows for timely adjustments to new pedagogical approaches while ensuring that students are not left to falter.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: v. Shared  understanding  and  dialogue: Sweden  and  Netherlands  make  their  SQA feedback accessible to education stakeholders while focusing on learners' progress and needs. In Ireland, reports on all but incidental inspections are published in a manner that disallows formation of league tables. England's Office for Standards in Education (OfSTED) mandates institutions  to  circulate  a  copy  of  the  assessment  report  to  all registered parents at the school within stipulated days of receipt of the final report.

texts.orig: 12.4.2 McKinsey and Company (2010) perspectives on standards and QA system
texts.text: 12.4.2 McKinsey and Company (2010) perspectives on standards and QA system

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The report ' How the World's Most Improved School Systems Keep Getting Better' by McKinsey  and  Company  (2010) describes  a  system-oriented  SQA  model  that  clusters interventions differently for schools, as they progress from poor to fair, to good, to great, and onto excellent performance. The McKinsey model is based on analysis of 20 education systems globally,  all  with  improving  but  differing  performance  levels;  examining  how  each  has achieved significant and sustained gains in learning outcomes on international and national assessments. Consideration is given to: (a) what it takes to ignite system change, (b) strategies that  facilitate  breakthrough, (c) interventions  that  build  cumulative  momentum, (d) how to sustain the improvement; and (e) how to move to the next developmental stage.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Taskforce recommends a system-oriented model that shifts the focus of SQA away from a tight alignment to structures and use of narrowly defined standards to system innovation and continuous  improvement  while  integrating  both  internal  and  external  SQA  strategies.  The proposed system blends standards and SQA perspectives around the set of integrated critical
texts.text: The Taskforce recommends a system-oriented model that shifts the focus of SQA away from a tight alignment to structures and use of narrowly defined standards to system innovation and continuous  improvement  while  integrating  both  internal  and  external  SQA  strategies.  The proposed system blends standards and SQA perspectives around the set of integrated critical

texts.label: text
texts.orig: performance-level appropriate actions; and in-builds an institutional-level SQA culture through self-assessment and reporting (see Appendix/Table 12.1). A system-oriented model encourages school-based professional development through action research, innovation, communities of learning, peer networking, and transfer of learning. In addition, the model encourages handholding (coaching); builds teamwork and active collaborations amongst institutions, professionals and education stakeholders as well as leverages on various forms of technical expertise to ensure continuous improvement in education quality.

texts.orig: The  Taskforce  observed  that  the  moderating  role  of  SQA  bears  critical  implications  for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 -to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all; and the MoE's vision and mission (provide quality, relevant and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development). While  taking cognizance of the lengthy reporting structure, the Taskforce therefore recommends:
texts.text: The  Taskforce  observed  that  the  moderating  role  of  SQA  bears  critical  implications  for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 -to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all; and the MoE's vision and mission (provide quality, relevant and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development). While  taking cognizance of the lengthy reporting structure, the Taskforce therefore recommends:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: i. A reporting structure with concurrent (administrative and functional) accountability to the CS Education, PS State Department of Early Learning and Basic Education and the DG. Given the DQAS mandate as the internal education standards and quality audit representative of the MoE, such direct accountability to the MoE senior management will fast track decisions on education SQA; allow uninhibited appraisal and reporting of SQA findings without influence from the auditees; and ensure timely feedback and attention to the concerns of SQA.
texts.text: A reporting structure with concurrent (administrative and functional) accountability to the CS Education, PS State Department of Early Learning and Basic Education and the DG. Given the DQAS mandate as the internal education standards and quality audit representative of the MoE, such direct accountability to the MoE senior management will fast track decisions on education SQA; allow uninhibited appraisal and reporting of SQA findings without influence from the auditees; and ensure timely feedback and attention to the concerns of SQA.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ii. Integration of the team culture within the broader National and decentralized education management and administration processes. The team formation has ability to surmount the  rigidity  and  high-level  formality  that  prevailed  in  education  management.  This would ensure a flexibly functional relationship between the MoE and TSC; enhance collaboration and information sharing; and leverage on different forms of expertise by sharing key people, for complementarity and synergy while enhancing innovation and improvement of education.

The figure shows administrative and functional reporting relationships in which the DQAS will account to multiple authority levels,  and implies that the directorate's  performance will be overseen at different supervision levels. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 13.1 Introduction
texts.text: 13.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter presents a discussion on governance, financing, accountability and Information Communication and Technology (ICT) integration in the Education sector in the context of the Competency based Curriculum (CBC) reforms. It is organised in four main sections beginning with definition of key concepts, followed by a situational analysis based on review of relevant literature. The next section analyses insights from stakeholder submissions and engagements while the final section makes key recommendations.

texts.orig: 13.2 Key Concepts
