texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 13.2.1 Governance
texts.text: 13.2.1 Governance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Governance takes various forms: as a structure which refers to the formal and informal set of institutions  involved  in  the  CBC  and  education  delivery;  as  a  process  which  refers  to  the dynamics  and  leading  functions  that  take  place  in  the  process  of  policy  making;  as  a mechanism which refers to institutional procedures of decision making as well as compliance and control; and, as a strategy which refers to manipulation of institutional and mechanical design with the aim of influencing choices and preferences.
texts.text: Governance takes various forms: as a structure which refers to the formal and informal set of institutions  involved  in  the  CBC  and  education  delivery;  as  a  process  which  refers  to  the dynamics  and  leading  functions  that  take  place  in  the  process  of  policy  making;  as  a mechanism which refers to institutional procedures of decision making as well as compliance and control; and, as a strategy which refers to manipulation of institutional and mechanical design with the aim of influencing choices and preferences.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Forberger (2014) and; Kaufmann, Kraay & Mastruzzi (2004; 2007) define governance as the 'traditions  and  structures  by  which  authority  in  an  institution  is  exercised  for  the  common good', which includes the process of selecting those in authority, capacity of the government to manage, and respect for the set regulations. While desirable and perhaps necessary for the economic and social well-being of institutions, these factors need to be supported to ensure effective provision of education.
texts.text: Forberger (2014) and; Kaufmann, Kraay & Mastruzzi (2004; 2007) define governance as the 'traditions  and  structures  by  which  authority  in  an  institution  is  exercised  for  the  common good', which includes the process of selecting those in authority, capacity of the government to manage, and respect for the set regulations. While desirable and perhaps necessary for the economic and social well-being of institutions, these factors need to be supported to ensure effective provision of education.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Good governance of education denotes responsiveness, accountability, transparency, engagement of citizens and the capacity of state actors (central and local Government decision makers) to design and implement the envisaged policies. Governance in education encompasses  creation  of  a  system  of  measuring  how  institutions  conduct  and  manage educational affairs while utilizing available resources efficiently. This entails decision-making, oversight and ethical practices with regard to how the resources and processes are actualized towards desired outputs and outcomes.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 13.2.2 Financing
texts.text: 13.2.2 Financing

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Financing of education and training is the process of budgetary allocation to ensure equitable distribution of resources to all sectors in education. The Jomtien Declaration on Education for All (UNESCO, 1990), the Dakar Framework for Action (UNESCO, 2000) and the 2015 Addis Ababa Declaration on Financing of Education, assert that governments should spend at least 20 per cent of their national budget or at least 6 per cent of their Gross National Product (GNP) on education. In addition, governments are urged to ensure cost-effectiveness in the use of the budgeted resources to realise quality education for all. As a signatory to these protocols, Kenya allocates about 6 per cent of her Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to education. Kenya has also enacted laws, policies and regulations that promote accountability in financial management.

texts.orig: 13.2.3 Accountability
texts.text: 13.2.3 Accountability

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Accountability in education is the state of being answerable to the stakeholders in education for the resources used in education (NOUN, 2008). According to Adams, Hill, Lichtenberger, Perkins and Shaw (1967), accountability is concerned with determining what records are to be kept, how such records will be maintained in terms of procedures, methodology and forms to be  used,  in  recording  classification  and  summary  of  activities  or  events,  analysis  and interpretation of the recorded data; preparation and issuing reports and statements which reflect conditions at a given time.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Accountability  in  education  emphasizes  building  more  inclusive,  equitable,  good-quality education systems and practices. Accountability cannot succeed without an enabling environment that provides actors with the resources, capacity, motivation and information to fulfil their responsibilities (UNESCO, 2017). To achieve the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 of ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities  for  all,  all  education  sector  actors  must  make  concerted  efforts  to  meet  their responsibilities.

texts.orig: Insights from global practices indicate that participatory governance in the Philippines and Niger  has  led  to  improved  and  effective  governance  in  their  education  systems.  The  two countries have strengthened the use of government-sponsored training to enhance parents and school participation  in  school  governance  (Ling,  Khattri,  &  Jha,  2020; Koazuka,  2018). texts.orig: In the Republic of Macedonia, decentralization is a relatively novel trend and local Government institutions  are  still  trying  to  adjust  to  the  new  conditions  and  responsibilities  (UNESCO, 2010).  In  a  decentralized  environment,  the  Ministry  of  Education  and  Science  sets  the education policy at a central level. Education  services are delivered locally by the Municipalities in cooperation with the local communities or associations of parents, teachers, and students that are represented on the school board - a management body through which school-based  management  is  ensured.  The  governance  model  is  intended  to  increase  the democratic development in the Country by enhancing involvement of the private sector and the civil society in decision-making, policy making and implementation of education.

texts.orig: Further, the Ministry of Education (MoE) has set up structures at the County and Sub-County levels, with clearly defined governance and accountability roles; and these ensure involvement of  various  stakeholders  and  institutions. texts.text: 13.3.5 Financing of Education and Training in Kenya

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Article 53 (1) (b) of the Constitution of Kenya guarantees every Kenyan child the right to free and compulsory Basic Education. The main source of funds for public Education and Training is the Government of Kenya (GoK) through National Treasury whose main revenue resources include domestic taxes, external and internal loans and grants from development partners. The amount voted to education is determined by the growth of the economy that is dependent on resource mobilization and support from development partners and donors. The private sector supplements Government efforts through Public Private Partnerships.

texts.text: 13.3.6 Financing Education and Training in the context of CBC

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The CBC is a response to the Constitutional commitment by the Government under Article 43 (1) (f) Article 53 (1) (b) and Article 55 (a). In this regard the MoE will continue to ensure effective implementation of the curriculum reforms and affirmative action programmes such as hiring and  remuneration  of  human  resource,  provision  of  teaching  materials  and improvement  of  infrastructure;  which  all  have  funding  implications.  Implementation  of curriculum  reforms  will  require  effective  resource  mobilization;  rationalization  of  resource utilization and adoption of sustainable financing mechanisms. It would however be important that a detailed analysis is undertaken aimed at establishing the realistic needs-based unit cost of all levels of education (Pre-primary, Primary, JSS, SSS, SNE, Teacher Education, TVET and University Education) in the context of CBC that considers equity and quality.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Increasing public financing alone is not adequate given the envisaged expansion of Secondary education both in the medium term and long term while targeting 100 per cent transition and the constitutional provisions on ensuring access to compulsory quality Basic Education that covers Pre-primary, Primary and Secondary education; as well as SNE. In 2020, private school enrolments  constituted  15  per  cent  of  the  total  Secondary  education  enrolment.  Feasible financing  options  could  include  private  sector  expansion  of  physical  infrastructure  and contributions towards the proposed Secondary education scholarship fund at County and Subcounty level, targeting the poor and vulnerable groups in society.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This Taskforce established that majority of Secondary schools are day schools (65.5 per cent) accommodating  55.2  per  cent  of  the  learners  in  Secondary  education.  Comparing  the proportions across school categories, 12.4 per cent of these are private schools accommodating about 5.4 per cent of the total enrolment, while 87.6 per cent are public schools accommodating 94.6  per  cent  of  the  enrolments.  This  in  part,  indicates  that  any  cost  effective  strategy  in Secondary education would have to target expansion of day schools. Boarding schools would however be justified only in areas with sparse population distribution such as the Arid and Semi- Arid Lands (ASAL). A selection of special needs learners would also require boarding facilities while inclusive education will take priority. A larger proportion of enrolments at SSS could be ensured by increasing the number of day students even in boarding schools.

texts.orig: For sustainability,  Kenya would need  such cost-effective financing options to cater for the envisaged  enrolment  expansion. For  instance,  students  who  are  likely  not  to  benefit  from formal Secondary schooling could be provided with access to Secondary education through alternative methods such as distance learning and skills training. Another option would be to strengthen  partnerships  with  other  stakeholders  such  as  County  Governments,  the  private sector, Non- Governmental Organizations (NGOs), and communities; and, to institutionalize incentives to induce such a Framework. texts.orig: 13.4 Insights from Global Practices on ICT Integration in Education
texts.text: 13.4 Insights from Global Practices on ICT Integration in Education

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  2020  edition  of  the  World  Summit  on  the  Information  Society  (WSIS)  -  Millennium Development Goals (MDG) Plan of Action aimed at building an inclusive information society and promotion of use of ICTs for achievement of the development goals envisaged in the WSIS Plan of Action. The Plan also sought to address new challenges related to integration of ICTs at the national, regional and international levels. Specific targets for the WSIS Plan of Action to  be  achieved  by  2015  included  connecting  villages  with  ICTs  through  establishment  of community  access  points;  linking  Universities,  colleges,  Secondary,  Primary,  Pre-primary schools; and, scientific and research centres with ICTs.
texts.text: The  2020  edition  of  the  World  Summit  on  the  Information  Society  (WSIS)  -  Millennium Development Goals (MDG) Plan of Action aimed at building an inclusive information society and promotion of use of ICTs for achievement of the development goals envisaged in the WSIS Plan of Action. The Plan also sought to address new challenges related to integration of ICTs at the national, regional and international levels. Specific targets for the WSIS Plan of Action to  be  achieved  by  2015  included  connecting  villages  with  ICTs  through  establishment  of community  access  points;  linking  Universities,  colleges,  Secondary,  Primary,  Pre-primary schools; and, scientific and research centres with ICTs.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Other targets included connecting public libraries, cultural centres, museums, post offices and archives with ICT; linking health centres and hospitals with ICTs; fast-tracking ICTs to all local  and  central  Government  departments;  establishing  websites  and  email  addresses;  and adapting all Primary and Secondary school curricula to meet the challenges of ICT, taking into account the specific national circumstances. Indeed, the Plan aims at ensuring that the entire world population has access to television, radio services, ICT and internet. The fundamental objective of the Plan is to ensure that everyone has necessary skills to benefit fully from the fruits of the information society.

texts.orig: The UNESCO ICT Competency Framework for Teachers was developed to support Countries to establish policies and standards that provide guidelines for national teacher ICT competency. Further,  although  ICT  competency  in  itself  may  not  necessarily  enhance  its  integration  by teachers into the instructional processes, it is aimed at providing an important component for Governments to develop legal frameworks for the integration of ICT in Education Masterplans (Olsson,  2006).  The  Framework  has  three  different  approaches  to  developing  teachers' competencies.  These  are:  development  of  technology  literacy,  knowledge  deepening  and, creation of knowledge .

texts.text: 13.4.1 ICT Integration in CBC Implementation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Kenya has made significant progress towards developing digital literacy and use of ICTs in the education, training and  research  Sub-sectors.  The  MoE  adopted  the  Digital  Literacy Programme (DLP) where schools were provided with digital resources to support curriculum delivery at the lower Primary level.  However, the challenges faced in use of the tablets by schools include unreliable electricity supply, unreliable and/or lack of internet connection, lack of  ICT skills  among teachers; in some  cases, unwillingness of teachers to integrate ICT in teaching and learning, and, unsustainability of the programme.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Through joint implementation, the Ministries of Education, ICT and Energy have connected approximately  90  per  cent  of  the  public  Primary  schools  to  electricity,  and  supplied  DLP resources in 99 per cent of the public Primary schools (ICT Authority 2017). These include about 900,000 Learner Digital Devices (LDD), 45,000 Teacher Digital Devices (TDD), 21,000 Content  Access  Points  and  19,500  projectors.  Digital  content  was  also  developed  and distributed to all public Primary schools in all the subject areas, including those aligned to the CBC; for learners in Grades 1 and 2. Capacity building under the DLP resulted in the training of  over  93,000  teachers  and  Curriculum  Support  Officers  (CSOs)  to  support  the  DLP programme and integration of ICT and assistive technology for learners with special needs.

texts.text: 13.4.2 ICT Integration in Education in the context of Curriculum Reforms

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To  enhance  use  of  ICTs  in  teaching,  learning,  assessment  and  management,  a  number  of initiatives  are  paramount. These include teacher training; improved broadband connectivity especially in rural and peri-urban areas; enhanced coordination among the different players and development of a comprehensive policy and strategy on ICT integration in education that is hinged on the National ICT policy (2019). Similarly, while investments have been directed towards deploying ICTs in education, there is need to generate evidence on the impact of these interventions. Whereas some schools have made considerable progress in integrating ICTs, there are considerable regional disparities in the use of ICTs.

Further, minimal investment and opportunities was noted for learners with disabilities and special needs.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 14.1 Introduction
texts.text: 14.1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter discusses the role of communication for implementation of the curriculum reforms in Kenya. It is organised in three main sections excluding this introduction. The first section expounds  the  concept  of  communication  and  related  terminologies.  Next  is  a  situational analysis of communication in education followed by recommendations on practical strategies of effective communication that will enhance understanding, appreciation and achievement of desirable  results  through  well-designed  programmes  of  advocacy,  public  mobilization  and stakeholder management on issues related to the Competency based Curriculum (CBC). The final  section  provides  recommendations  on  how  communication  on  CBC  reforms  will  be implemented to enhance public and stakeholder awareness, participation and ownership.

texts.orig: 14.2 Key Concepts
texts.text: 14.2 Key Concepts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The term communication is commonly used to imply relaying of information. However, in a technical sense, communication denotes a field of study practised under clearly defined norms and ethos. Scholars such as Shannon and Weaver (1949) define communication broadly as all the procedures by which people may influence another through written and oral speech, music, pictorial  arts,  theatre,  ballet  and  other  human  behaviour.  Rodrique  (1992)  asserts  that communication is an exchange and exact replication of thoughts, feelings, facts, beliefs and ideas  between  and  among  individuals  through  a  common  system  of  symbols  to  influence actions or behaviour change.
texts.text: The term communication is commonly used to imply relaying of information. However, in a technical sense, communication denotes a field of study practised under clearly defined norms and ethos. Scholars such as Shannon and Weaver (1949) define communication broadly as all the procedures by which people may influence another through written and oral speech, music, pictorial  arts,  theatre,  ballet  and  other  human  behaviour.  Rodrique  (1992)  asserts  that communication is an exchange and exact replication of thoughts, feelings, facts, beliefs and ideas  between  and  among  individuals  through  a  common  system  of  symbols  to  influence actions or behaviour change.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The chapter applies the term communication in three interrelated ways; namely, the interactions and  engagements  which  take  place  among  different  actors;  transmission  of  information, knowledge or data between two or more points (Saywell & Cotton, 1999); the processes and means through which these interactions take place. From the foregoing, the Taskforce defines communication  as  the  process  of  formulating  and  exploring  schematic  models  of  relaying information with the aim of influencing actions in the context of curriculum implementation as a long-term 'process' of rolling out certain bits of messages that target specific audiences. The definition assumes that communication encompasses information flow, transfer, transmission or transaction.

Successful partnerships emerge when most of the parties see themselves and the others as moving in the same direction, working for similar interests, sharing the same  meanings  about  educational issues, reforms, programs  etc. Communication can help build trust. texts.orig: The situational analysis discusses how previous Education Commissions, Working Parties and Taskforces have addressed the issue of communication for education reforms. It is guided by insights and recommendations of the Ominde Report (GoK, 1965); Gachathi Report (GoK, 1976); MacKay Report (GoK, 1981) and Kamunge Report (GoK, 1988). The Kamunge Report (GoK, 1988) highlights communication strategies on the Government of Kenya (GoK) and MoE  initiatives,  the  challenges  in  communication;  while  also  providing  a  rationale  for communication in the education reforms.

texts.text: 14.3.2 Successful use of Communication in MoE initiatives

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ministry of Education (MoE) has considerable potential to effectively deploy communication in rallying stakeholders to support Government reforms as noted in the robust communication to embrace the 100 per cent transition policy  for  learners  from  Primary  to Secondary education. The same potential is noted in advocating for the successful enrolment of learners in National Education Management Information System (NEMIS).

texts.orig: 14.3.4 Rationale for Communication in the Implementation of Curriculum Reforms
texts.text: 14.3.4 Rationale for Communication in the Implementation of Curriculum Reforms

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Arguably, effective communication of the curriculum reforms is fundamental for rallying the support  of  stakeholders  and  the  general  public  around  the  rationale  of  the  reforms  and  its implementation  process  with  the  aim  of  facilitating  consensus  and  confidence  building, advocacy and campaigns as well as for public and social mobilization, as explained below. In this context, ensuring that communication is founded on accurate information and verifiable facts is the foundation of the success of intended outcomes.

In this context, ensuring that communication is founded on accurate information and verifiable facts is the foundation of the success of intended outcomes.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 14.3.4.1 Accurate information sharing
texts.text: 14.3.4.1 Accurate information sharing

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Sustained  and  accurate  messages  guided  by  a  well-designed  Communication  Strategy  has potential of reaching various audiences in ways that would facilitate articulation of the essence of  the  CBC  reforms  to  the  respective  stakeholders.  According  to  McQuail  (1994),  media institutions,  which  are  channels  for  communication,  are  essential  in  the  production  and distribution of knowledge which helps individuals to make sense of the social world around them. This anchors the reason why stakeholders need to access CBC information; enhance their knowledge and awareness as well as promote positive and responsive behaviour as a necessary connection with enhanced participation and engagement in the implementation and uptake of the reforms.

texts.orig: 14.3.4.2 Advocacy and campaigns
texts.text: 14.3.4.2 Advocacy and campaigns

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  purpose  of  advocacy  is  to  create  social  change.  Communication  for  social  change  is grounded  in  the  work  of  Freire  (1970),  who  conceived  communication  as  dialogue  and participation for the purpose of creating cultural identity, trust, commitment, ownership and empowerment.  Fraser  and Villet (1994) advance the argument that planned use of communication techniques, activities and media presents the people with powerful tools to experience change and guide its adoption.

texts.orig: studies  in  development  communication such as  Servaes (2008) and  Figueroa et  al. (2005), which  suggest  that  development  programmes  cannot  produce  change  without  ongoing, culturally  and  socially  relevant  dialogue  among  the  relevant  parties.  Thus,  it  is  noted  that effective implementation of the CBC will require dissemination of targeted messages to various stakeholders. In line with the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 (GoK, 2010), public communication will allow public participation leading to ownership.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As  conceptualized  in  the  BECF  (KICD,  2017),  the  CBC  has  remarkable  structural  and conceptual  proposals  that  depart  from  8-4-4  such  as  emphasis  on  formative  assessment, competencies,  talents  and  specialization,  hence  introduces  Pathways  and  Tracks  in  Senior Secondary School (SSS). The CBC also seeks to institutionalize Value-based Education (VbE), promote Community Service Learning (CSL), address the Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs), and ensure Parental  Engagement  and  Empowerment  (PEE).  Targeted  public communication and information are therefore vital in mobilizing parents, communities and stakeholders to appreciate and support proposed policy changes such as day schooling.

texts.orig: 14.3.4.4 Eliminating propaganda
texts.text: 14.3.4.4 Eliminating propaganda

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Scholars have interrogated propaganda in specific contexts and disciplines (Jowett & O'Donell, 2005; Thorton & Taithe, 1999; Parry-Giles, 2002). In its neutral sense, propaganda entails the 'propagation' through dissemination or promotion of particular ideas (Jowett and O'Donell, 2005).  However,  because  of  usage  across  diverse  fields  such  as  religion,  history,  military, sociology and psychology, propaganda has acquired different meanings that is largely negative.
texts.text: Scholars have interrogated propaganda in specific contexts and disciplines (Jowett & O'Donell, 2005; Thorton & Taithe, 1999; Parry-Giles, 2002). In its neutral sense, propaganda entails the 'propagation' through dissemination or promotion of particular ideas (Jowett and O'Donell, 2005).  However,  because  of  usage  across  diverse  fields  such  as  religion,  history,  military, sociology and psychology, propaganda has acquired different meanings that is largely negative.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Propaganda commonly connotes lies, distortion, deceit, manipulation, mind-control, psychological warfare and brainwashing. In communication, propaganda is understood to mean news  management,  spinning  or  selective  content  dissemination  to  shape  information  in  a particular way by giving emphasis on certain elements, negative or positive, depending on the intention of the source but with the goal of influencing the audience in certain direction (Carey, 1997; Jowett & O'Donell, 2006).

texts.orig: 14.3.4.5 Communication Strategy
texts.text: 14.3.4.5 Communication Strategy

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  section  provides  a  strategy  for  communication  on  CBC.  It  recognises  that  effective communication  is  vital  for  successful  implementation  of  the  CBC.  Therefore,  it  seeks  to eliminate  propaganda,  misinformation,  disinformation  and  fake  information,  which  have potential to derail reform agenda. The strategy seeks to address the following: accuracy of information  on  CBC;  enhanced  advocacy  and  public  campaigns;  stakeholder  engagement; developing  key  messages;  providing  targeted  communication  to  various  audiences.  It  also highlights potential risks and the consequential mitigation measures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This chapter presents an implementation Framework of key recommendations derived from the various chapters of this Taskforce report. The Framework aligns the key recommendations with proposed  implementation  activities,  timelines  for  the  envisaged  deliverables,  means  of verification and the actors responsible for the outputs. texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A Ignore the matter; it is really not that important.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B Punish the learner.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C Ask the learner to move back to their sitting position.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D Report the matter to the head teacher or class teacher for action.
texts.text: D Report the matter to the head teacher or class teacher for action.

texts.label: list_item

texts.text: When you catch a learner making funny gestures behind your back.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A Slap the learner; punishment must be as close to the infringement as possible.
texts.text: A Slap the learner; punishment must be as close to the infringement as possible.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B Ask the learner to account for his actions in front of the class.
texts.text: B Ask the learner to account for his actions in front of the class.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C Talk to the learner, preferably in private after, to explain the seriousness of the offence.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B Ask the learner to sit down immediately.

texts.orig: C Remind the learner the class rules and ask them to act appropriately.
